Preparativi.2.full: Complete the standard setup for {0} players as shown in the rulebook. *Note that the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} track and starting player will be set by the Storybook in the coming pages.*

Preparativi.4.full: This unofficial scenario uses some components from the **The Cost of Disease** Scenario Box. Keep it close at hand, but **do not open it**: the Storybook will tell you which components to take, and when. Everything else must stay in the box, unseen.

Prologo.2.full: **Dr Ferenc Halász – Society for Psychical Research, Budapest – *3 March 1923.***

Prologo.4.full: I write to you from the village I told you of, where I arrived on the evening train with an umbrella that proved entirely useless. The parish priest, a kind and very tired man, handed me the keys to the old sacristy. Behind a walnut wardrobe was a door, crudely bricked up; behind the door, six crates of documents.
Prologo.4.easy: I am writing to you from the village I told you about. I arrived on the evening train, with an umbrella that did not help at all. The parish priest, a kind and very tired man, gave me the keys to the old sacristy. Behind a wooden wardrobe there was a door closed up with bricks. Behind the door there were six crates full of documents.
Prologo.4.short: I write from the village I told you of. The priest gave me the keys to the old sacristy: behind a bricked-up door were six crates of documents.

Prologo.5.full: Séance minutes, letters never sent, torn diary pages, cuttings from the local gazette, telegrams whose ink has long since faded to violet. They cover fifty years and three generations of a single family: scientists, or something they liked to call by that name, who for half a century tried to speak with the dead. And not, it would seem, always without an answer.
Prologo.5.easy: There are séance records, letters that were never sent, torn diary pages, articles from the local newspaper and old telegrams. They tell the story of fifty years and three generations of the same family: scientists, or so they called themselves, who for half a century tried to talk to the dead. And it seems that sometimes someone answered.
Prologo.5.short: Minutes, letters, diaries and telegrams: fifty years of a family of scientists who tried to speak with the dead. And sometimes, it seems, were answered.

Prologo.6.full: I have resolved to sort and transcribe them before forming any judgement. The first document is the record of a wake. I ask you to read it as I did: with the scepticism the Society demands, and with the window shut.
Prologo.6.easy: I decided to put the documents in order and copy them before I judge anything. The first document is about a wake. I ask you to read it the way I did: with the doubt the Society asks for, and with the window closed.
Prologo.6.short: I have sorted and copied them. The first is the record of a wake: read it with scepticism, and with the window shut.

PreparaFolla.1.full: Place the Suspicion Marker on space **{0}** and the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} marker one space to its left. Give the {icon:StartPlayerToken} marker to **{1}**.

Traguardi.2.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.5.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.8.full: The first time a player reaches Level 2 of the Occult Journal Track this Generation,

Traguardi.11.full: The first time a player reaches 15VP this Generation,

PosaTraguardi.2.full: Place one on **space 3** of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track, one on **space 3** of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and one on **space 15** of the Victory Point Track. The fourth goes at the top of the **Level 2 column of the Occult Journal Track**: it counts for every player.

PosaTraguardi.3.full: When a player's marker reaches one of these tokens, that player clicks the matching entry in the Storybook and reads a message. Then the token returns to the supply.

TkCreepy.2.full: For some days now, when you walk through {0}, people cross themselves. Children stop playing, dogs lower their tails. At night, under your window, there are bare footprints that lead up to the wall and never come back. Whatever it is, it has decided that you are the most interesting person in town.
TkCreepy.2.easy: For some days now, when you walk through {0}, people make the sign of the cross. Children stop playing and dogs lower their tails. At night, under your window, there are bare footprints: they go up to the wall and do not come back. Something has decided that you are the most interesting person in town.
TkCreepy.2.short: In {0} people cross themselves as you pass. Under your window, bare footprints lead to the wall and never come back. Something has chosen you.

TkCreepy.3.full: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift. Better not to wonder where it came from.
TkCreepy.3.easy: One morning you find a gift in front of your door. It is better not to ask where it comes from.

TkCreepy.4.full: In the fog you are never without company. A light step follows you, always three metres behind, and stops when you stop. The lanterns lean towards you like flowers towards the sun, and the estate dog will no longer sleep in your room. In the village they say you carry the Presences with you, the way other people carry a smell.
TkCreepy.4.easy: In the fog you are never without company. A light step follows you, always three metres behind, and stops when you stop. The lanterns lean towards you like flowers towards the sun, and the estate dog will not sleep in your room any more. In the village they say you carry the Presences with you, the way other people carry a smell.
TkCreepy.4.short: In the fog a light step always follows you. The village says you carry the Presences with you.

TkCreepy.5.full: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift wrapped in a sheet wet with fog. Better not to ask where it came from.
TkCreepy.5.easy: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift wrapped in a sheet wet with fog. Better not to ask where it came from.
TkCreepy.5.short: On the doorstep you find a gift in a wet sheet. Better not to ask where it came from.

TkCreepy.6.full: The Gazette has printed your photograph in an article on "families who talk to the dead", and since then everyone in town recognises you. Ladies cross the street, the tram conductors do not make you pay, children follow you at a distance singing a rhyme about the veil. At night, under the window, there are bare footprints on the wet cobbles.
TkCreepy.6.easy: The Gazette has printed your photograph in an article about "families who talk to the dead", and since then everyone in town knows you. Ladies cross the street, the tram conductors let you ride free, children follow you singing a rhyme about the veil. At night, under the window, there are bare footprints on the wet cobbles.
TkCreepy.6.short: Since your photo in the Gazette, the whole town knows you. At night there are bare footprints under your window.

TkCreepy.7.full: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift, with a note: *"From the one who watches you."*
TkCreepy.7.easy: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift with a note: *"From the one who watches you."*
TkCreepy.7.short: On the doorstep, a gift: *"From the one who watches you."*

TkCreepy.9.full: You keep it, and take it to the laboratory.

TkCreepy.10.full: You take it to the cemetery and bury it.

TkCreepy.11.full: In the laboratory, under the lamp, the gift turns out to be useful, and exactly as unsettling as you expected. You say thank you aloud, out of politeness. Someone behind the door seems pleased.
TkCreepy.11.easy: In the laboratory, under the lamp, the gift turns out to be useful, and just as unsettling as you thought. You say thank you aloud, to be polite. Someone behind the door seems pleased.
TkCreepy.11.short: The gift is useful, and unsettling. You say thank you. Someone behind the door is pleased.

TkCreepy.12.full: Gain 1 {icon:Bodies_Icon}. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkCreepy.13.full: You bury it in a corner of the cemetery, at night, with a prayer you half remember. The next morning the footprints under your window are gone. In their place, on the sill, there is a smooth white pebble, like the ones children leave on graves.
TkCreepy.13.easy: You bury it in a corner of the cemetery, at night, with a prayer you half remember. The next morning the footprints under the window are gone. In their place, on the sill, there is a smooth white pebble, like the ones children leave on graves.
TkCreepy.13.short: You bury it at night. Next day the footprints are gone, and a white pebble sits on the sill.

TkCreepy.14.full: Gain 1VP. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.2.full: At first it is only a murmur, like a room full of people in the house next door. Then you make out the words. Then the voices: an old woman looking for a ring, a child who counts to a hundred and starts again, a man who keeps repeating the same address. None of them seems to know they are dead.
TkInsanity.2.easy: At first you hear only a murmur, like many people in a room of the house next door. Then you understand the words. Then you hear the voices: an old woman looking for a ring, a child who counts to a hundred and starts again, a man who always repeats the same address. None of them seems to know they are dead.
TkInsanity.2.short: First a murmur, then voices: an old woman seeking a ring, a child counting, a man repeating an address. None of them knows they are dead.

TkInsanity.3.full: The voices come with the fog, and with the fog they do not go away. They speak German, Hungarian, a country tongue nobody uses any more. A woman asks you every evening whether you have seen her son; a soldier asks you the way to a village burned forty years ago. Some of the voices you recognise: you heard them at the table as a child, when the grown-ups thought you were asleep.
TkInsanity.3.easy: The voices come with the fog, and they do not leave. They speak German, Hungarian, a country tongue nobody uses any more. A woman asks you every evening if you have seen her son; a soldier asks you the way to a village that burned forty years ago. Some voices you know: you heard them at the table as a child, when the grown-ups thought you were asleep.
TkInsanity.3.short: With the fog come the voices, and they stay. Some you know: you heard them at the table as a child.

TkInsanity.4.full: You hear them in the hum of the electric wires, in the whistle of the train, in the needle of the café phonograph when the record has finished and turns on empty. Hundreds of voices, thousands, polite and patient as a crowd in a waiting room. Each is waiting its turn to tell you something. Some, it seems to you, have waited fifty years.
TkInsanity.4.easy: You hear them in the hum of the electric wires, in the train whistle, in the needle of the café phonograph when the record has ended and spins on empty. Hundreds of voices, thousands, polite and patient like a crowd in a waiting room. Each one waits its turn to tell you something. Some, it seems to you, have waited fifty years.
TkInsanity.4.short: You hear voices in the wires, the train, the phonograph. Thousands of them, patient. Each wants to tell you something.

TkInsanity.7.full: You stop your ears with wax.

TkInsanity.8.full: You take notes. You could not say whether you do it for science or to make them be quiet.

TkInsanity.9.full: Gain 1 Occult Knowledge. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.10.full: You warm the wax of a candle between your fingers and fill your ears with it, like the sailors in the story. The silence is so sudden that your head spins. For three days you hear nothing: not the voices, not the rain, not the people talking to you at table. On the fourth day you take out the wax, and the voices are gone. For now.
TkInsanity.10.easy: You warm candle wax between your fingers and fill your ears with it, like the sailors in the story. The silence is so sudden that your head spins. For three days you hear nothing: not the voices, not the rain, not the people talking to you at table. On the fourth day you take the wax out, and the voices are gone. For now.
TkInsanity.10.short: You stop your ears with wax. After three days of silence, the voices are gone. For now.

TkInsanity.11.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkOccult.2.full: One morning you open the Journal and find a page you did not write. The handwriting slants backwards, the ink is still wet, and the formula it describes is wrong in one place only, as if whoever wrote it wanted to see whether you would notice.
TkOccult.2.easy: One morning you open the Journal and find a page you did not write. The handwriting leans backwards and the ink is still wet. The formula on the page has only one mistake, as if the writer wanted to see if you would notice.
TkOccult.2.short: In the Journal is a page you did not write, the ink still wet, with a single mistake, like a test.

TkOccult.3.full: The second volume of the Journal has one page too many. Yesterday it was not there: you know because you counted them, all of them, the evening before. It is written in two hands, your grandfather's and that of the one who brought you into the world, taking turns line by line as in a conversation. The formula at the bottom is wrong in one place only.
TkOccult.3.easy: The second volume of the Journal has an extra page. It was not there yesterday: you know because you counted them all the evening before. It is written in two hands, your grandfather's and your parent's, one line each, like a conversation. The formula at the bottom is wrong in one place only.
TkOccult.3.short: There is a new page in the Journal, written by your grandfather and your parent. The formula has a single mistake.

TkOccult.4.full: Among the pages of the Journal, which are now three and a half volumes, there is a sheet typed on the bone keys of the Telegraph: you recognise it by the slightly crooked letters. Nobody has switched the machine on. The sheet describes an experiment, carefully and impatiently, and it is wrong in one place only.
TkOccult.4.easy: Among the pages of the Journal, which now fill three and a half volumes, there is a sheet typed on the Telegraph's bone keys: you know it by the slightly crooked letters. No one has switched the machine on. The sheet describes an experiment, carefully and impatiently, and it has only one mistake.
TkOccult.4.short: In the Journal is a sheet typed by the Telegraph, though no one switched it on. The experiment has a single mistake.

TkOccult.6.full: You correct the mistake on the page.

TkOccult.7.full: You tear out the page and burn it.

TkOccult.8.full: You notice. Beneath the correction, someone has added a single word: *"Good."*
TkOccult.8.easy: You notice. Under your correction, someone has written one word: *"Good."*

TkOccult.9.full: Draw an Experiment from the deck of your choice. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkOccult.10.full: The page burns badly, in fits and starts, like damp paper. When it is ash, in its place in the Journal there is a torn margin with three words written crosswise: *"Pity. Another time."* But the formula, the right one, you have worked out by now on your own.
TkOccult.10.easy: The page burns badly, in fits and starts, like damp paper. When it is ash, a torn margin is left in the Journal with three words written crosswise: *"Pity. Another time."* But by now you have worked out the right formula yourself.
TkOccult.10.short: You burn it. On the torn margin is written: *"Pity. Another time."* But you have worked out the right formula.

TkOccult.11.full: Gain 2VP. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkVP.2.full: Your name is going round {0}: at the market, in church, in the taverns. Some say it with fear, others with admiration, all of them in a low voice. A few days later a black-edged card invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves"; inside the envelope, as a courtesy, there is money.
TkVP.2.easy: In {0} everyone talks about you: at the market, in church, in the taverns. Some are afraid, others admire you, but they all speak quietly. A few days later you receive a card with a black border: it invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves". Inside the envelope, as a kindness, there is money.
TkVP.2.short: All {0} is talking about you, quietly. A black-edged card invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves", with money inside.

TkVP.3.full: The ladies of the Circle greet you by name, the notables offer you their seat at the café, the village doctor writes about you to a colleague in Vienna. A few days later a black-edged card arrives: an invitation "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves, in the fog, as in the old days"; inside the envelope, as a courtesy, there is some money.
TkVP.3.easy: The ladies of the Circle greet you by name, the important people give you their seat at the café, the village doctor writes about you to a colleague in Vienna. A few days later a black-edged card arrives: an invitation "to a dinner among people who will not give up, in the fog, as in the old days". In the envelope, as a courtesy, there is some money.
TkVP.3.short: Everyone knows you. A black-edged card arrives: an invitation to dinner, and some money.

TkVP.4.full: The Budapest newspaper gives you a short paragraph, with a pen drawing that is not much of a likeness. In town people ask you for autographs, advice, a good word with the dead. A few days later a black-edged card arrives: an invitation "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves, like your family for three generations"; inside the envelope, as a courtesy, there is some money.
TkVP.4.easy: The Budapest newspaper writes about you, with a drawing that does not look much like you. In town people ask you for autographs, advice, a good word with the dead. A few days later a black-edged card arrives: an invitation "to a dinner among people who will not give up, like your family for three generations". In the envelope, as a courtesy, there is some money.
TkVP.4.short: The Budapest paper writes about you. A black-edged card arrives: an invitation to dinner, and some money.

TkVP.5.full: The wax seal is black, with an open eye.

TkVP.8.full: You send back the invitation, and the money.

TkVP.9.full: The dinner is in a house with closed shutters, by candlelight. The guests are kind, well dressed, and eat nothing. Nobody asks you to sign anything; they only ask about your family, with affectionate interest, the way one asks after distant relatives. When it is time to leave you notice that every guest has beside them an empty place, laid for dinner.
TkVP.9.easy: The dinner is in a house with closed shutters, by candlelight. The guests are kind, well dressed, and eat nothing. No one asks you to sign anything; they only ask about your family, fondly, the way one asks about distant relatives. As you leave you notice that each guest has an empty place laid beside them.
TkVP.9.short: The guests are kind and eat nothing. Each has an empty place laid beside them.

TkVP.10.full: Gain $2. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkVP.11.full: You send the envelope back without a note, the seal unbroken. The next day it is brought back to you, unopened too, with a single line on the back: *"The place stays laid."* Word goes round the village that you said no to the Circle; someone shakes your hand in the street.
TkVP.11.easy: You send the envelope back without a note, the seal unbroken. The next day it comes back to you, also unopened, with one line on the back: *"The place stays laid."* The village says you turned down the Circle, and someone shakes your hand in the street.
TkVP.11.short: You send it back. It returns: *"The place stays laid."*

G1Intro.3.full: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead, under a thin rain that could not make up its mind to fall. The village came to the cemetery in good numbers, but stayed on the far side of the low wall: no one would go near the grave, and the gravedigger worked quickly, without looking in. It was said the old man had spent his last years shut up in the estate with machines that hummed through the night, and that from the windows of his laboratory there sometimes came a light of a colour no one could name.
G1Intro.3.easy: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead, under a light rain. Many people from the village came to the cemetery, but they stayed behind the low wall: no one wanted to go near the grave, and the gravedigger worked fast without looking in. People said that in his last years the old man had stayed shut up in the estate, with machines that made noise at night. Sometimes, from the windows of his laboratory, came a light of a strange colour that no one could describe.
G1Intro.3.short: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead. The village kept behind the cemetery wall: people said the old man had worked at night on humming machines, amid lights of a nameless colour.

G1Intro.4.full: The heirs had arrived on the coach the evening before, each from a different city, each with a trunk and the same letter from the notary. The estate was theirs, and with it the debts, the instruments, the animals in their cages and Father's Journal: a leather-bound notebook swollen with notes, sketches and formulae. On the last page he had written there was a single sentence, underlined twice, so hard that the pen had cut the paper:
G1Intro.4.easy: The heirs had arrived the evening before by coach. Each came from a different city, with a trunk and the same letter from the notary. Now the estate was theirs, and so were the debts, the instruments, the animals in the cages and Father's Journal: a leather notebook full of notes, drawings and formulae. On the last page there was only one sentence, underlined twice, so hard that the pen had cut the paper:
G1Intro.4.short: The heirs inherited the estate, the debts, the laboratory and Father's Journal. On its last page, one sentence, underlined so hard it cut the paper:

G1Intro.5.full: *"Death is not a closed door: it is a veil. And veils can be lifted."*

G1Intro.6.full: Father Anzelm blessed the body, closed his prayer book and told the heirs, loudly enough for everyone to hear, that he would pray for their souls with particular devotion.
G1Intro.6.easy: Father Anzelm blessed the body and closed his prayer book. Then he told the heirs, loudly enough for everyone to hear, that he would pray very hard for their souls.
G1Intro.6.short: Father Anzelm blessed the body and promised, loudly, to pray hard for the heirs' souls.

G1Intro.7.full: That night, in the estate, something began to knock on the walls.

G1ColpiA.4.full: I cannot sleep. The room they gave me was our father's: the bed still holds the shape of his body, and the air smells of camphor and acid. I put out the candle an hour ago when I hear the first knock.
G1ColpiA.4.easy: I cannot sleep. They gave me our father's room: the bed still has the shape of his body and the air smells of camphor and acid. I put out the candle an hour ago, and then I hear the first knock.
G1ColpiA.4.short: I lie awake in our father's room. Then I hear the first knock.

G1ColpiA.5.full: It comes from the wall behind the headboard. A sharp knock, like a knuckle on wood. Then two. Then one. Then nothing, for so long that I almost convince myself I dreamt it; and then they begin again, always the same, patient, like someone knocking at a door who knows there is someone at home.
G1ColpiA.5.easy: The sound comes from the wall behind the bed. A sharp knock, like a knuckle on wood. Then two knocks. Then one. Then nothing, for so long that I almost think I dreamt it. Then they start again, always the same and patient, like someone knocking at a door who knows someone is home.
G1ColpiA.5.short: Knocks on the wall behind the bed: one, two, one. Then silence, and again, patient, like someone who knows you are home.

G1ColpiA.6.full: In his library I saw a little French book on talking tables: one knock for yes, two for no. It comes back to me now, in the dark, and I wish it had not.
G1ColpiA.6.easy: In his library I saw a little French book about talking tables: one knock means yes, two mean no. I remember it now, in the dark, and I wish I did not.
G1ColpiA.6.short: I remember a little book from his library: one knock for yes, two for no. I wish I did not.

G1ColpiA.10.full: Pull the pillow over your head.

G1ColpiA.11.full: I sit up in bed and knock once, just once, with my knuckle, on the cold wall.

G1ColpiA.13.full: I ask, in the lowest voice, whether it is him. One knock. I ask whether he is at peace. Two knocks, so hard that the jug trembles on the chest of drawers. Then silence, and a smell of wax, though there is no candle lit in the room. In the morning my fingers are numb and the Journal lies open on the pillow, at a page I do not remember ever reading.
G1ColpiA.13.easy: I ask, very quietly, if it is him. One knock. I ask if he is at peace. Two knocks, so strong that the jug shakes on the chest of drawers. Then silence, and a smell of wax, even though no candle is lit in the room. In the morning my fingers are numb and the Journal is open on the pillow, at a page I do not remember ever reading.
G1ColpiA.13.short: Is it him? One knock. Is he at peace? Two knocks, very hard. In the morning the Journal lies open on my pillow, at a page I never read.

G1ColpiA.15.full: I wake the servant and send him to the village with the lantern. Father Anzelm arrives an hour later, his stole over his nightshirt and holy water in an apothecary's bottle. He blesses the wall, the bed, the window and, to be thorough, me as well.
G1ColpiA.15.easy: I wake the servant and send him to the village with the lantern. Father Anzelm arrives an hour later, with his stole over his nightshirt and holy water in a chemist's bottle. He blesses the wall, the bed, the window and, to be safe, me too.
G1ColpiA.15.short: I send for Father Anzelm. He comes in his nightshirt and blesses the wall, the bed and, to be thorough, me.

G1ColpiA.16.full: The knocking stops at once. The priest, however, lingers on the threshold longer than he needs to, looking around: the cages, the alembics, the Journal open on the table. Before leaving he shakes my hand and leaves me a few coins "for the household, until everything is in order". It feels more like a down payment than charity.
G1ColpiA.16.easy: The knocking stops at once. But the priest stays at the door longer than he needs to and looks around: the cages, the glass instruments, the Journal open on the table. Before he leaves he shakes my hand and gives me a few coins "for the household, until everything is in order". It feels more like an advance than help.
G1ColpiA.16.short: The knocking stops. The priest looks around a long time, then leaves me a few coins "for the household". It feels like a down payment.

G1ColpiA.18.full: I slip under the covers and press the pillow over my ears, as we did as children during storms. The knocking goes on for a long time, muffled, and at some point it seems to move: from the wall to the floor, from the floor to the headboard, a hand's breadth from my ear. Then, at last, it stops.
G1ColpiA.18.easy: I get under the covers and press the pillow on my ears, as we did as children during storms. The knocking goes on for a long time, more softly. At some point it seems to move: from the wall to the floor, from the floor to the bed, very close to my ear. Then, at last, it ends.
G1ColpiA.18.short: Under the covers, pillow over my ears, I hear the knocking creep closer, right up to my ear. Then at last it stops.

G1ColpiA.19.full: At dawn I draw back the curtain. On the wall, at the height of my head, the plaster has worn away in a small, regular circle, as if rubbed by a knuckle that had knocked there for years.
G1ColpiA.19.easy: At dawn I open the curtain. On the wall, at the height of my head, the plaster is worn away in a small, regular circle, as if a knuckle had knocked there for years.
G1ColpiA.19.short: At dawn there is a small worn circle on the wall, as if a knuckle had knocked there for years.

G1ColpiFine.2.full: At breakfast no one mentions the knocking. The coffee is too strong, the bread is yesterday's and everyone has dark rings under their eyes. Someone makes a joke about the mice in the attic, and no one laughs.
G1ColpiFine.2.easy: At breakfast no one talks about the knocking. The coffee is too strong, the bread is old and everyone looks tired. Someone makes a joke about the mice in the attic, but no one laughs.
G1ColpiFine.2.short: At breakfast no one mentions the knocking, and no one laughs at the jokes about mice.

G1ColpiFine.3.full: From the dining-room window you can see the village: a few wooden houses huddled around the church, smoke from the chimneys, the market waking up. It is a poor, suspicious place. But Father has left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people lower their voices; and a name, for those who know how to use it, is worth as much as capital.
G1ColpiFine.3.easy: From the dining-room window you can see the village: a few wooden houses near the church, smoke from the chimneys, the market opening. It is a poor place where people do not trust strangers. But Father has left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people speak quietly. And a name, if you know how to use it, is worth a lot of money.
G1ColpiFine.3.short: The village is poor and suspicious. But Father left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people lower their voices: capital, for those who know how to use it.

G1ColpiFine.4.full: What do you suggest, at breakfast?

G1ColpiFine.5.full: That the priest be called to bless the house.

G1ColpiFine.6.full: That the knocking be studied with method, as Father would have done.

G1ColpiFine.7.full: Nothing: you change the subject and talk about the weather.

G1ColpiFine.8.full: The suggestion falls into the silence like a spoon on the floor. Then someone nods, and someone else shrugs. Father Anzelm comes that same afternoon, blesses every room, even the laboratory cages, and leaves with the air of a man who has patched a coat that will not last.
G1ColpiFine.8.easy: The suggestion falls into the silence like a spoon on the floor. Then someone nods, and someone else shrugs. Father Anzelm comes that same afternoon, blesses every room, even the laboratory cages, and leaves looking like someone who has patched a coat that will not last.
G1ColpiFine.8.short: Father Anzelm blesses every room, but leaves looking as if he knows it will not be enough.

G1ColpiFine.10.full: The suggestion goes down better than you expected: after all you are scientists, or the children of one. In an afternoon Father's bedroom becomes an observatory: a pendulum clock, a notebook with columns for the hour, the number of knocks and the wall, a silk thread stretched from one wall to the other with three little bells. That night all three bells ring, in the right order.
G1ColpiFine.10.easy: The idea goes down better than you thought: after all you are scientists, or a scientist's children. In one afternoon Father's bedroom becomes an observatory: a pendulum clock, a notebook with columns for the hour, the knocks and the wall, a silk thread from one wall to the other with three little bells. That night all three ring, in the right order.
G1ColpiFine.10.short: Father's room becomes an observatory, with a thread and three bells. That night all three ring.

G1ColpiFine.12.full: You talk about the weather, the roads, the price of firewood. The others follow you with relief. It is a long, polite, utterly useless conversation; and by the end of breakfast everyone knows, without needing to say it, that tonight nobody will blow out the candle.
G1ColpiFine.12.easy: You talk about the weather, the roads, the price of firewood. The others follow you, relieved. It is a long, polite, completely useless conversation; and by the end of breakfast everyone knows, without saying so, that tonight no one will blow out the candle.
G1ColpiFine.12.short: You talk about the weather. But everyone knows no one will blow out the candle tonight.

G1R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **The Cost of Disease** section ({icon:S1_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 1**.

G1R1.19.full: A caravan has stopped at the edge of the village. They say a woman travels in it who talks with the dead, and that the dead answer her.
G1R1.19.easy: A caravan has stopped near the village. People say that a woman travels in it who talks to the dead, and that the dead answer her.
G1R1.19.short: The wagon of a woman who talks with the dead has come to the village.

G1R1.20.full: Click here at the end of the Round to move on to the next Round...

G1Tubo.2.full: The earth on Father's grave is still fresh, and from the middle of the mound sticks out a brass tube as thick as a wrist, closed with a screw cap and topped with a little bell. The gravedigger, a big, silent man called Mihály, takes off his cap before explaining.
G1Tubo.2.easy: The earth on Father's grave is still fresh. From the middle of the mound comes a brass tube as thick as a wrist, closed with a screw cap, with a little bell on top. The gravedigger, a big, quiet man called Mihály, takes off his cap before he explains.
G1Tubo.2.short: A brass tube with a bell comes out of Father's grave. Mihály the gravedigger explains.

G1Tubo.3.full: "The deceased's instructions," he says. "Written in his own hand and paid to the notary in advance. The tube goes down to the coffin, level with the mouth. If the gentleman wakes up, he can call; if he has no breath to call, there is the bell cord, tied to his wrist. Forty days it must stay open. Then it can be closed." He puts his cap back on. "I have buried plenty of gentlemen who were afraid of being buried alive. This is the first who seemed afraid of the opposite."
G1Tubo.3.easy: "The dead man's instructions," he says. "Written by him and paid to the notary in advance. The tube goes down to the coffin, level with his mouth. If the gentleman wakes, he can call; if he has no breath, there is the bell cord, tied to his wrist. It must stay open forty days. Then it can be closed." He puts his cap back on. "I have buried many gentlemen who were afraid of being buried alive. This is the first who seemed afraid of the opposite."
G1Tubo.3.short: "If the gentleman wakes, he can call up the tube or ring the bell. It stays open forty days. This one seemed afraid of the opposite of being buried alive."

G1Tubo.5.full: You come back at night and put your ear to the tube.

G1Tubo.6.full: You have the tube sealed with lead.

G1Tubo.7.full: You leave everything as it is, for forty days.

G1Tubo.8.full: At night the cemetery is smaller than by day: the graves crowd together, the low wall comes closer. You unscrew the cap and kneel in the mud. Cold air rises from the tube, smelling of wax and earth. At first you hear nothing; then, very far down, three faint knocks, like a fingernail on wood. One. Two. One.
G1Tubo.8.easy: At night the cemetery seems smaller: the graves crowd together, the low wall comes closer. You unscrew the cap and kneel in the mud. Cold air rises from the tube, smelling of wax and earth. At first you hear nothing; then, far down, three very faint knocks, like a fingernail on wood. One. Two. One.
G1Tubo.8.short: At night you open the tube. From deep down come three faint knocks. One. Two. One.

G1Tubo.9.full: Then a voice, so low it could be the wind in the brass, says a single word that you do not understand. You screw the cap back on with shaking hands. On the bell, when you stand up, there is a drop of dew that does not fall.
G1Tubo.9.easy: Then a voice, so low it could be the wind in the brass, says one word that you do not understand. You screw the cap back on with shaking hands. When you stand up there is a drop of dew on the bell that does not fall.
G1Tubo.9.short: Then a voice says a word you do not understand. You close the tube with shaking hands.

G1Tubo.11.full: The smith pours the lead into the tube in front of you and Father Anzelm, who wanted to be there and blesses the pouring the way one blesses a bell. The molten metal goes down gurgling, then stops, and for a moment a long hiss comes out of the tube, like someone holding their breath. The smith says it is the air. The priest says nothing.
G1Tubo.11.easy: The smith pours the lead into the tube in front of you and Father Anzelm, who wanted to be there and blesses it the way one blesses a bell. The molten metal goes down gurgling, then stops, and for a moment a long hiss comes out of the tube, like someone holding their breath. The smith says it is the air. The priest says nothing.
G1Tubo.11.short: The smith seals the tube with lead. A long hiss comes out of it. The priest says nothing.

G1Tubo.12.full: The bell you take off yourself, and carry home wrapped in a handkerchief. You put it in a drawer of the writing desk. All winter it never rings in the drawer; and all winter, every evening, you open the drawer to check.
G1Tubo.12.easy: You take the bell off yourself and carry it home in a handkerchief. You put it in a drawer of your desk. All winter it never rings; and all winter you open the drawer every evening to check.
G1Tubo.12.short: You keep the bell in a drawer. It never rings, but you check every evening.

G1Tubo.14.full: You leave the tube open, as Father wanted, and give Mihály a coin to check the bell every morning. For thirty-nine days the gravedigger comes to the estate, takes off his cap and says: "Nothing."
G1Tubo.14.easy: You leave the tube open, as Father wanted, and give Mihály a coin to check the bell every morning. For thirty-nine days the gravedigger comes to the estate, takes off his cap and says: "Nothing."
G1Tubo.14.short: You leave the tube open. For thirty-nine days Mihály comes to say: "Nothing."

G1Tubo.15.full: On the fortieth day he does not come. You find him at the cemetery, sitting on the grave, pale. The bell is still, he says; it has not rung. But last night, for the first time, someone unscrewed the cap from the inside. Then, to thank you for your patience, he quietly offers you a favour of the trade: something from the paupers' grave that nobody will come to claim.
G1Tubo.15.easy: On the fortieth day he does not come. You find him at the cemetery, sitting on the grave, pale. The bell has not rung, he says. But last night, for the first time, someone unscrewed the cap from the inside. Then, to thank you for your patience, he quietly offers you a favour of the trade: something from the common grave that no one will come looking for.
G1Tubo.15.short: On the fortieth day, the cap has been unscrewed from inside. Mihály offers you something from the common grave.

G1Fabbro.2.full: In the smithy, while you wait for your horse to be shod, you hear a rhythm you know. It comes from behind the forge: one knock, two, one. Then a pause. Then again: one, two, one. Behind the forge there is a boy of six or seven, with singed hair and a little hammer in his hand, patiently tapping on the side of the anvil.
G1Fabbro.2.easy: At the smithy, while you wait for your horse to be shod, you hear a rhythm you know. It comes from behind the forge: one knock, two, one. A pause. Then again: one, two, one. Behind the forge is a boy of six or seven, with singed hair and a little hammer, patiently tapping on the side of the anvil.
G1Fabbro.2.short: At the smithy you hear a rhythm you know: one, two, one. A little boy is beating it on the anvil.

G1Fabbro.3.full: His name is Jóska, and he is the smith's son. He explains, very seriously, that at night from his bed he hears knocking from the other side of the river, from the big house, and that he answers, so that whoever is knocking does not feel alone. His father grabs him by the ear and apologises: the boy has too much imagination, and the big house, with respect, makes too much noise.
G1Fabbro.3.easy: His name is Jóska, and he is the smith's son. He explains, very seriously, that at night in bed he hears knocking from across the river, from the big house, and that he answers, so the one knocking does not feel alone. His father takes him by the ear and says sorry: the boy has too much imagination, and the big house, with respect, makes too much noise.
G1Fabbro.3.short: Jóska, the smith's son, says that at night he answers the knocking from the big house, so it won't feel alone.

G1Fabbro.5.full: You give him a coin and ask him to teach you the game.

G1Fabbro.6.full: You tell his father to make him stop.

G1Fabbro.7.full: Jóska teaches you the game with the self-important air of a schoolmaster. One knock is yes, two is no, but everybody knows that; the beauty of it, he says, is that if you wait long enough the knocks become letters, and the letters words. He shows you his: a row of notches on the wood of the door, counted night after night.
G1Fabbro.7.easy: Jóska teaches you the game with the important air of a teacher. One knock is yes, two is no, but everyone knows that; the best part, he says, is that if you wait long enough the knocks become letters, and the letters words. He shows you his: a row of notches on the door, counted night after night.
G1Fabbro.7.short: Jóska teaches you that, with patience, knocks become letters and words. He shows you the notches on his door.

G1Fabbro.8.full: When you leave he asks if you will come back. You say yes. His father, touched, fills your pockets with offcuts of metal he no longer needs.
G1Fabbro.8.easy: When you leave he asks if you will come back. You say yes. His father, touched, fills your pockets with bits of metal he no longer needs.
G1Fabbro.8.short: You promise to come back. His father gives you scraps of metal.

G1Fabbro.10.full: The smith takes the little hammer from his son and sends him indoors with a cuff round the ear. The boy does not cry. He stops on the threshold and looks at you for a long time, dry-eyed, the way one looks at someone one wants to remember.
G1Fabbro.10.easy: The smith takes the hammer from his son and sends him inside with a cuff on the ear. The boy does not cry. He stops in the doorway and looks at you for a long time, dry-eyed, as if he wants to remember you.
G1Fabbro.10.short: The smith sends the boy indoors. He does not cry, and looks at you as if to remember you.

G1Fabbro.11.full: The smith, mortified, will not be paid for the horse. That night, at the estate, the knocking on the walls is louder and faster than usual, like that of someone who knocks and gets no answer.
G1Fabbro.11.easy: The smith, embarrassed, will not take money for the horse. That night, at the estate, the knocking on the walls is louder and faster than usual, like someone knocking with no one answering.
G1Fabbro.11.short: That night the knocking at the estate is louder, like someone knocking with no answer.

G1Carro.2.full: Madame Vámos is in the village, comforting a widow. Her caravan stands at the edge of the wood, the horses grazing and the door ajar, as if someone had left it open on purpose. Inside it is dark, and there is a smell of incense, of horse and of something sweeter, like flowers left too long in water.
G1Carro.2.easy: Madame Vámos is in the village, comforting a widow. Her caravan is standing at the edge of the wood, the horses grazing and the door ajar, as if someone had left it open on purpose. Inside it is dark, and it smells of incense, of horse, and of something sweeter, like flowers left too long in water.
G1Carro.2.short: Madame is in the village. Her caravan door is ajar, as if left open on purpose.

G1Carro.3.full: There is a round table covered with a velvet cloth, four chairs, a portrait turned to face the wall and, under the bunk, a trunk with iron corners. Nobody sees you. You have time to look at one thing, perhaps two.
G1Carro.3.easy: There is a round table covered in velvet, four chairs, a portrait turned to the wall and, under the bunk, a trunk with iron corners. No one sees you. You have time to look at one thing, maybe two.
G1Carro.3.short: Inside are a table and a trunk. You have time to look at one thing.

G1Carro.8.full: Under the cloth the table has a single leg, hollow, with a wooden lever just sticking out of the floor: a pedal, at the height of the foot of whoever sits in the medium's place. And from the top a black silk thread hangs down, very fine, disappearing into a hole in the floorboards.
G1Carro.8.easy: Under the cloth the table has a single hollow leg, with a wooden lever just sticking out of the floor: a pedal, right where the foot of whoever sits in the medium's chair would be. And from the top a very fine black silk thread hangs down and disappears through a hole in the floor.
G1Carro.8.short: Under the table is a pedal, and a black silk thread that vanishes into the floor.

G1Carro.9.full: It is a trick, and a well-made one. You are still admiring it when the table, though nobody has touched the pedal, knocks once against the floor. You leave the caravan in a great hurry. But at home you draw the mechanism from memory.
G1Carro.9.easy: It is a trick, and a good one. You are still admiring it when the table, though no one has touched the pedal, knocks once on the floor. You run out of the caravan. But at home you draw the mechanism from memory.
G1Carro.9.short: It is a trick. But the table knocks once by itself, and you flee. At home you draw the mechanism.

G1Carro.11.full: The trunk is not locked. Inside there are shawls, packs of cards, a phial of phosphorus and a bundle of letters tied with black ribbon. You recognise the handwriting at once: it is the Journal's. They are letters from your father, addressed to *"Eszter"*, and the dates run from 1821 to a few months ago.
G1Carro.11.easy: The trunk is not locked. Inside are shawls, packs of cards, a phial of phosphorus and a bundle of letters tied with a black ribbon. You know the handwriting at once: it is the Journal's. They are letters from your father to *"Eszter"*, dated from 1821 to a few months ago.
G1Carro.11.short: In the trunk are letters from your father to *"Eszter"*, from 1821 to a few months ago.

G1Carro.12.full: You read just one, the first that comes to hand: it speaks of an experiment, of a door, of a promise that "we shall see each other again, one way or another". It is dated three weeks after the funeral. You put everything back, the ribbon knotted as it was, and for days you cannot get it out of your head.
G1Carro.12.easy: You read only one, the first you find: it speaks of an experiment, a door, and a promise: "we shall see each other again, one way or another". It is dated three weeks after the funeral. You put everything back, the ribbon tied as before, and for days you cannot think of anything else.
G1Carro.12.short: One letter promises: "we shall see each other again, one way or another". It is dated after the funeral.

G1Carro.14.full: You close the caravan door and walk away. On the path you meet Madame Vámos, coming back from the village with her basket on her arm. She looks at your hand, the one you closed the door with, and smiles.
G1Carro.14.easy: You close the caravan door and leave. On the path you meet Madame Vámos, coming back from the village with her basket on her arm. She looks at your hand, the one that closed the door, and smiles.
G1Carro.14.short: You leave. On the path you meet Madame, who looks at your hand and smiles.

G1Carro.15.full: "You are a well-mannered person," she says. "Your father, at your age, was not." Then she puts in your palm a very old silver coin, with a likeness you do not recognise, "for when you want to come back". You do not know if it is a compliment or a down payment.
G1Carro.15.easy: "You are a polite person," she says. "Your father, at your age, was not." Then she puts in your hand a very old silver coin, with a face you do not know, "for when you want to come back". You cannot tell if it is a compliment or a down payment.
G1Carro.15.short: "You are polite. Your father was not." She gives you an old coin, "for when you want to come back".

G1Codicillo.2.full: In the notary's office, on the first floor of the Town Hall, there is a smell of damp paper and tobacco. The notary is a slight man with a slightly crooked wig, and he has the air of someone who must read something he would rather not have found. It is a codicil to Father's will, written in his own hand, which arrived by post from Vienna a week after the funeral.
G1Codicillo.2.easy: In the notary's office, on the first floor of the Town Hall, it smells of damp paper and tobacco. The notary is a small man with a slightly crooked wig, and he looks like someone who has to read something he would rather not have found. It is an addition to Father's will, in his own hand, which came by post from Vienna a week after the funeral.
G1Codicillo.2.short: The notary reads an addition to Father's will, which came from Vienna a week after the funeral.

G1Codicillo.3.full: *"Let my room stay as it is: the bed, the papers, the lamp, the chair beside the bed. Let nothing be moved and let the window not be opened as long as someone, in that room, goes on knocking. Afterwards, do as you please."* The notary looks up from the sheet. "The law does not oblige you," he says. "But if I were you, I would think about it."
G1Codicillo.3.easy: *"Let my room stay as it is: the bed, the papers, the lamp, the chair by the bed. Let nothing be moved and the window not be opened as long as someone, in that room, keeps knocking. After that, do as you like."* The notary looks up from the page. "The law does not make you," he says. "But in your place I would think about it."
G1Codicillo.3.short: *"Let my room stay as it is as long as someone there keeps knocking."* "The law does not make you," says the notary. "But I would think about it."

G1Codicillo.5.full: You respect the codicil: the room stays as it is.

G1Codicillo.6.full: You have the room cleared and turn it into a laboratory.

G1Codicillo.7.full: The room stays as it was: the bed with the shape of the body, the lamp unlit, the chair beside the bed, always pulled out a little, as if someone had just sat in it. The housekeeper refuses to dust it. You go in now and then, in the evening, and each time the chair is closer to the bed.
G1Codicillo.7.easy: The room stays as it was: the bed with the shape of the body, the lamp out, the chair by the bed, always pulled out a little, as if someone had just sat in it. The housekeeper will not dust it. You go in now and then, in the evening, and each time the chair is closer to the bed.
G1Codicillo.7.short: The room stays as it was. Each time you go in, the chair is closer to the bed.

G1Codicillo.9.full: You have everything taken away in one afternoon: the bed to the attic, the papers to the study, the chair to the kitchen. When they lift the mattress, underneath there are dozens of folded sheets, dense with notes, dated with Father's last nights. At the bottom of the last one, a line larger than the others: *"They answer."*
G1Codicillo.9.easy: You have it all taken away in one afternoon: the bed to the attic, the papers to the study, the chair to the kitchen. Under the mattress there are dozens of folded sheets, full of notes, with the dates of Father's last nights. At the bottom of the last one is a line bigger than the rest: *"They answer."*
G1Codicillo.9.short: Under the mattress are the notes of Father's last nights. The last line says: *"They answer."*

G1Codicillo.10.full: That night, in the empty room, nobody knocks. They knock in the kitchen, against the chair.
G1Codicillo.10.easy: That night, in the empty room, no one knocks. They knock in the kitchen, against the chair.
G1Codicillo.10.short: That night they knock in the kitchen, against the chair.

G1Dagherrotipo.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, among the baskets of cabbages, a travelling photographer has set up a stand with a black cloth and a box of silver plates. His name is Koch, he comes from Pest, and he makes portraits of the living and the dead: the dead cost more, he says, because they keep still better, but they have to be held up with an iron rod behind the back.
G1Dagherrotipo.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market, among the baskets of cabbages, a travelling photographer has a stand with a black cloth and a box of silver plates. His name is Koch, he comes from Pest, and he takes portraits of the living and the dead: the dead cost more, he says, because they keep still better, but they must be propped up with an iron rod behind the back.
G1Dagherrotipo.2.short: At the market the photographer Koch takes portraits of the living and the dead. The dead cost more.

G1Dagherrotipo.3.full: When he hears your surname his face lights up. Three months before the funeral, he says, he took a portrait of your father, at the estate, and was never paid. He shows you the plate: Father seated, thin, with the Journal on his knees and an empty chair beside him. And in the polished silver, if you tilt it against the light, on the empty chair there is a woman in a black shawl.
G1Dagherrotipo.3.easy: When he hears your surname his face lights up. Three months before the funeral, he says, he took a portrait of your father at the estate, and was never paid. He shows you the plate: Father sitting, thin, with the Journal on his knees and an empty chair beside him. And in the silver, if you tilt it to the light, on the empty chair sits a woman in a black shawl.
G1Dagherrotipo.3.short: Koch has a portrait of your father, never paid for. Tilt the plate, and on the empty chair beside him sits a woman in a black shawl.

G1Dagherrotipo.6.full: You ask the photographer who the woman was.

G1Dagherrotipo.7.full: You ask him to destroy the plate, and pay him to do it.

G1Dagherrotipo.8.full: You pay your father's debt, with interest, and take the portrait home wrapped in a cloth. You hang it in the study. By day the chair beside Father is empty. In the evening, with the lamp lit, not always.
G1Dagherrotipo.8.easy: You pay your father's debt, with interest, and take the portrait home wrapped in a cloth. You hang it in the study. By day the chair beside Father is empty. In the evening, with the lamp lit, not always.
G1Dagherrotipo.8.short: You hang the portrait in the study. By day the chair is empty. In the evening, not always.

G1Dagherrotipo.10.full: The photographer scratches his head. There was no woman in the room, he says: there was himself, the gentleman, and the empty chair, which the gentleman insisted on having beside him, "for a friend who will come". The pose lasted two minutes. Halfway through, the gentleman smiled. That is why, in the portrait, his mouth is a little blurred.
G1Dagherrotipo.10.easy: The photographer scratches his head. There was no woman in the room, he says: only himself, the gentleman, and the empty chair, which the gentleman insisted on having beside him, "for a friend who will come". The pose took two minutes. Halfway through, the gentleman smiled. That is why his mouth is a little blurred in the portrait.
G1Dagherrotipo.10.short: "There was no woman," says Koch. "The gentleman wanted the empty chair, for a friend who would come. Halfway through the pose he smiled."

G1Dagherrotipo.12.full: The photographer hesitates, then rubs the plate with a rag soaked in cyanide, in front of you. The silver clouds over, Father disappears, the chair disappears. Last of all the woman disappears, and it seems to you, though it is surely a trick of the light, that she has time to turn towards you.
G1Dagherrotipo.12.easy: The photographer hesitates, then wipes the plate with a rag soaked in cyanide, in front of you. The silver clouds over, Father vanishes, the chair vanishes. The woman vanishes last, and it seems to you, though it must be the light, that she has time to turn towards you.
G1Dagherrotipo.12.short: The plate is wiped clean. The woman vanishes last, and seems to turn towards you.

G1Seduta.3.full: Madame Vámos's wagon is painted midnight blue and covered in flaking gold stars. It has tall wheels, velvet curtains and, on the door, an open hand with an eye in its palm. It has stood at the edge of the village for three weeks, and in three weeks half the widows of {0} have climbed into it at least once, behind the priest's back.
G1Seduta.3.easy: Madame Vámos's wagon is painted dark blue and covered in worn gold stars. It has tall wheels, velvet curtains and, on the door, a picture of an open hand with an eye in the palm. It has been near the village for three weeks, and in that time half the widows of {0} have gone inside at least once, without telling the priest.
G1Seduta.3.short: Madame Vámos's wagon, midnight blue with a hand and an eye on the door, has stood there three weeks. Half the widows of {0} have secretly been inside.

G1Seduta.4.full: This morning the medium came to the estate in person. She is a small woman of indeterminate age, wrapped in a black shawl; she speaks softly, with an accent I cannot place, and has very white, very cold hands. She said she had heard the knocking. Not that someone had told her about the knocking: that she had *heard* it, from the road, passing the gate on the night of the dead.
G1Seduta.4.easy: This morning the medium came to the estate. She is a small woman, and it is hard to tell how old she is. She wears a black shawl, speaks softly with a strange accent, and has very white, very cold hands. She said she had heard the knocking. No one had told her about it: she had *heard* it herself, from the road, passing the gate on the night of the dead.
G1Seduta.4.short: The medium, small and ageless, came to the estate. She says she *heard* the knocking from the road, on the night of the dead.

G1Seduta.5.full: "Your father has something to say," she told us. "And he does not speak gladly to those who will not listen." Then she invited all of us to a séance in her wagon, tomorrow at midnight. She asked for no money. That, more than anything else, worries me.
G1Seduta.5.easy: "Your father has something to say," she told us. "And he does not like to speak to people who will not listen." Then she invited all of us to a séance in her wagon, tomorrow at midnight. She did not ask for money. That worries me more than anything.
G1Seduta.5.short: "Your father has something to say." She invited us to a séance tomorrow at midnight, free of charge. That is what worries me.

G1SedutaVoto.2.full: Each player takes a Voting token and chooses in secret. When everyone has chosen, reveal your votes together.

G1SedutaVoto.3.full: YAY: you attend Madame Vámos's séance.

G1SedutaVoto.4.full: NAY: you stay at the estate.

G1SedutaRacconto.2.full: No one goes. Madame Vámos lights the candles, sits at the little table and waits until dawn before empty chairs. The baker's boy, who passes by at four, swears he heard her talking to someone, and heard someone answer.
G1SedutaRacconto.2.easy: No one goes. Madame Vámos lights the candles, sits at the little table and waits until dawn in front of empty chairs. The baker's boy walks past at four and swears he heard her talking to someone, and heard someone answer.
G1SedutaRacconto.2.short: No one goes. Madame waits until dawn before empty chairs; the baker's boy swears he heard her talking, and someone answering.

G1SedutaRacconto.3.full: That night, at the estate, the knocking doubles. It knocks on every wall, every door, the headboard of every bed. It knocks like someone who has been left out in the cold.
G1SedutaRacconto.3.easy: That night, at the estate, there are twice as many knocks. They knock on every wall, every door, everyone's bed. They knock like someone who has been left outside in the cold.
G1SedutaRacconto.3.short: That night the knocking doubles, everywhere, like someone left out in the cold.

G1SedutaRacconto.4.full: All the heirs sit around the little round table, in the wagon that smells of incense and horse. Madame asks them to join hands; her fingers are icy. She recites something in a language no one recognises, then falls silent, and in the silence the table creaks, tilts and rises a hand's breadth off the floor, with every hand still upon it.
G1SedutaRacconto.4.easy: All the heirs sit around the little round table, in the wagon that smells of incense and horse. Madame asks them to hold hands; her fingers are freezing. She says something in a language no one knows, then she is silent. In the silence the table creaks, tips and rises a hand's width off the floor, with all their hands on it.
G1SedutaRacconto.4.short: The heirs join hands around the table. Madame recites unknown words, and the table rises a hand's breadth off the floor.

G1SedutaRacconto.5.full: It stays suspended for the space of a breath. Then it drops with a single, sharp knock. Madame opens her eyes and smiles like someone who has just had good news. "He recognised you," she says. "All of you."
G1SedutaRacconto.5.easy: It stays in the air for the time of one breath. Then it falls with a single sharp knock. Madame opens her eyes and smiles, like someone who has just had good news. "He recognised you," she says. "All of you."
G1SedutaRacconto.5.short: The table drops with one knock. Madame smiles: "He recognised you. All of you."

G1SedutaRacconto.6.full: Only some of the heirs climb into the wagon. The others stay at the estate, in front of the fire, telling one another that someone in the family must keep a little common sense.
G1SedutaRacconto.6.easy: Only some of the heirs get into the wagon. The others stay at the estate, in front of the fire, and tell each other that someone in the family must have a little common sense.
G1SedutaRacconto.6.short: Only some of the heirs go; the others stay home, out of common sense.

G1SedutaRacconto.7.full: Around one in the morning, from the direction of the village, comes a scream. Then another. Then a laugh, which could be anyone's. Those who return at dawn will not say what they saw; but their hands are as cold as Madame's, and all morning they keep looking at the walls.
G1SedutaRacconto.7.easy: Around one in the morning, a scream comes from the village. Then another. Then a laugh, but it is not clear whose. Those who come back at dawn do not want to say what they saw. But their hands are as cold as Madame's, and all morning they look at the walls.
G1SedutaRacconto.7.short: In the night, screams and a laugh from the village. Those who return at dawn say nothing, their hands cold as Madame's, eyes on the walls.

G1SedutaRacconto.8.full: Those who voted YAY gain 1 Occult Knowledge and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}.

G1SedutaRacconto.9.full: Those who voted NAY move back 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track.

G1Patroni.3.full: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Last Sunday the Reverend Father Anzelm devoted his entire sermon to what he called, without mincing words, "the witch of the wagon". He reminded the faithful that the dead rest in the hands of God and not in the drawers of a little table, and that whoever disturbs them for money disturbs Him too. He then added, looking towards the pews at the back, that certain recently arrived families would do well to remember it.
G1Patroni.3.easy: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Last Sunday Father Anzelm spoke for the whole sermon about what he called, very clearly, "the witch of the wagon". He reminded the faithful that the dead rest with God, not inside a little table, and that whoever disturbs them for money also disturbs God. Then, looking at the pews at the back, he said that some families who had arrived recently should remember this.
G1Patroni.3.short: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Father Anzelm's sermon was about "the witch of the wagon": the dead rest with God, and certain newly arrived families would do well to remember it.

G1Patroni.4.full: The sermon was much appreciated. On Monday, however, this newspaper observed an unusual coming and going of ladies in black on the road to the estate. The widows of {0} have lost husbands, sons and brothers to the cold, the fevers and hunger; they want news of their loved ones, and for one's loved ones, as everyone knows, no expense is spared.
G1Patroni.4.easy: People liked the sermon very much. On Monday, however, this newspaper saw many ladies dressed in black coming and going on the road to the estate. The widows of {0} have lost husbands, sons and brothers to the cold, fevers and hunger. They want news of their loved ones, and for loved ones, as everyone knows, people pay gladly.
G1Patroni.4.short: On Monday, though, many widows of {0} take the road to the estate: they want news of their dead, and will pay for it.

G1Patroni.5.full: The cemetery's gravedigger, questioned by this newspaper, confirms that at night someone from the estate goes to listen at the brass tube sticking out of the old man's grave. He does not say what can be heard. He says that, since then, the bell no longer needs the wind.
G1Patroni.5.easy: The cemetery's gravedigger, questioned by this newspaper, confirms that at night someone from the estate goes to listen at the brass tube coming out of the old man's grave. He does not say what can be heard. He says that, since then, the bell no longer needs the wind.
G1Patroni.5.short: The gravedigger confirms: at night someone from the estate listens at the tube. And the bell rings without wind.

G1Patroni.6.full: The smith, who poured the lead into the tube of the old man's grave in the presence of the reverend, says he heard the metal hiss like a kettle. The reverend has asked him not to tell anyone.
G1Patroni.6.easy: The smith, who poured the lead into the tube of the old man's grave in front of the reverend, says he heard the metal whistle like a kettle. The reverend has asked him not to tell anyone.
G1Patroni.6.short: The smith says the lead in the tube whistled like a kettle.

G1Patroni.7.full: It is also reported that the smith's son, a boy of six, is going round the village teaching everyone a new game, which consists of knocking on walls in a certain order. Mothers are asked to keep an eye on their children.
G1Patroni.7.easy: It is also reported that the smith's son, a boy of six, is going round the village teaching everyone a new game: knocking on walls in a certain order. Mothers are asked to keep an eye on their children.
G1Patroni.7.short: The smith's son is teaching everyone to knock on walls. Mothers are asked to watch their children.

G1Patroni.8.full: Some say there is a pedal under the caravan table. Madame Vámos, when asked, invited whoever says so to sit in her place, and try.
G1Patroni.8.easy: Some say there is a pedal under the caravan table. Madame Vámos, when asked, invited whoever says so to sit in her place and try.
G1Patroni.8.short: Some talk of a pedal under the table. Madame invites them to try it.

G1Patroni.9.full: And your family, the following Sunday?

G1Patroni.10.full: Goes to Mass, in the front row.

G1Patroni.11.full: Opens the gate to the ladies in black.

G1Patroni.12.full: The family from the estate goes to Mass all together, in the front row, in their best clothes and with the faces of people who have not slept. Father Anzelm, from the pulpit, stares at them for a while and changes the end of his sermon: he speaks of the prodigal son. The ladies in black, at the back of the church, exchange glances.
G1Patroni.12.easy: The family from the estate goes to Mass all together, in the front row, in their best clothes and with the faces of people who have not slept. Father Anzelm, from the pulpit, stares at them for a while and changes the end of his sermon: he talks about the prodigal son. The ladies in black, at the back of the church, look at each other.
G1Patroni.12.short: You go to Mass in the front row. Father Anzelm changes his sermon to the prodigal son.

G1Patroni.14.full: On Sunday morning, while the bells are ringing, the family from the estate opens the gate. The ladies in black come up the road two by two, veils lowered, and sit in the great drawing room, under Father's portrait, to talk about their dead. None of you does anything special: you listen, that is all. The ladies leave at lunchtime, comforted. Father Anzelm, that Sunday, preaches to half a church.
G1Patroni.14.easy: On Sunday morning, while the bells ring, the family from the estate opens the gate. The ladies in black come up two by two, veils lowered, and sit in the big drawing room, under Father's portrait, to talk about their dead. None of you does anything special: you just listen. The ladies leave at lunchtime, comforted. That Sunday Father Anzelm preaches to half a church.
G1Patroni.14.short: You open the gate to the widows and listen to them talk of their dead. That Sunday the church is half empty.
