G1Banca.2.full: The Bank of {0} is a single room, with a brass grille, a safe as big as a wardrobe and a banker, Mr Weisz, who wears his sleeve protectors even on Sundays. He receives you with the embarrassment of someone who has news to give and does not know whether it is good.
G1Banca.2.easy: The Bank of {0} is a single room, with a brass grille, a safe as big as a wardrobe and a banker, Mr Weisz, who wears his sleeve protectors even on Sundays. He receives you awkwardly, like someone who has news to give and does not know if it is good.
G1Banca.2.short: Mr Weisz the banker receives you awkwardly: he has news for you.

G1Banca.3.full: Your father's account, he explains, did not close with his death. For twenty years, on the first of every month, a deposit has arrived from Vienna, always the same, signed only with three initials: **C. U. O.** It came this month too. "As if the sender," says Mr Weisz, adjusting his spectacles, "had not been informed. Or as if he did not consider it important."
G1Banca.3.easy: Your father's account, he explains, did not close when he died. For twenty years, on the first of each month, the same deposit has come from Vienna, signed only with three initials: **C. U. O.** It came this month too. "As if the sender," says Mr Weisz, straightening his glasses, "did not know. Or did not care."
G1Banca.3.short: For twenty years a monthly deposit signed **C. U. O.** has come into your father's account. It came this month too.

G1Banca.6.full: You have it all returned to the sender.

G1Banca.7.full: You ask the banker to see the signature.

G1Banca.8.full: Mr Weisz counts the notes twice, with wet fingers, and hands them to you in an envelope. That evening, emptying the envelope onto the laboratory table, out falls a note the banker swears he never saw. A single line, in an elegant, old-fashioned hand: *"For the family's expenses. There are always expenses, in a family."*
G1Banca.8.easy: Mr Weisz counts the notes twice, with wet fingers, and gives them to you in an envelope. That evening, as you empty the envelope onto the laboratory table, out falls a note the banker swears he never saw. A single line, in an elegant, old-fashioned hand: *"For the family's expenses. There are always expenses, in a family."*
G1Banca.8.short: In the envelope is a note: *"For the family's expenses. There are always expenses, in a family."*

G1Banca.10.full: You sign the order to return it, and Mr Weisz sends it to Vienna by Thursday's coach. On the first of the next month the deposit arrives on time, doubled, with a note from the sender: *"We insist."*
G1Banca.10.easy: You sign the order to send it back, and Mr Weisz sends it to Vienna by Thursday's coach. On the first of the next month the deposit arrives on time, doubled, with a note: *"We insist."*
G1Banca.10.short: You send it back. Next month it returns, doubled: *"We insist."*

G1Banca.11.full: You have it returned again. Word gets round, as all word does in {0}: the family from the estate turns down money, and in the village whoever turns down money is either a saint or has something to hide.
G1Banca.11.easy: You send it back again. Word gets round, as all word does in {0}: the family from the estate refuses money, and in the village anyone who refuses money is either a saint or has something to hide.
G1Banca.11.short: You send it back again. The village says whoever refuses money is a saint or has something to hide.

G1Banca.13.full: Mr Weisz hesitates, then opens the ledger. Beside each deposit, where the sender's signature should be, there is a small ink drawing: a carnation, carefully blacked in. Under the first, the one from 1828, there is also a name written in full: *O. Garai*.
G1Banca.13.easy: Mr Weisz hesitates, then opens the ledger. Beside each deposit, in place of a signature, there is a small ink drawing: a carnation, carefully blacked in. Under the first one, from 1828, there is also a full name: *O. Garai*.
G1Banca.13.short: Instead of a signature there is always a black carnation. Under the first, from 1828, is a name: *O. Garai*.

G1Banca.14.full: The latest deposit, this month's, bears the same drawing and the same name, in the same hand, with the same pressure of the pen. "A son, I imagine," says the banker. "Or a grandson. Respectable families hand down their signature, like the family silver."
G1Banca.14.easy: This month's deposit has the same drawing and the same name, in the same handwriting, pressed with the same force. "A son, I imagine," says the banker. "Or a grandson. Good families pass their signature down, like the silver."
G1Banca.14.short: This month's deposit has the identical signature. "A son, or a grandson," says the banker.

G1Vedova.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, among the baskets of eggs and the chicken cages, a woman dressed in black holds you back by the sleeve. It is Panna Kovács, the miller's widow. Her husband died of cholera last summer, in three days, without managing to say where he had hidden thirty years' savings; and she, with four children and a mill standing idle, sells her hens' eggs to pay for bread.
G1Vedova.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market, among the baskets of eggs and the chicken cages, a woman in black catches you by the sleeve. It is Panna Kovács, the miller's widow. Her husband died of cholera last summer, in three days, without being able to say where he had hidden thirty years of savings; and she, with four children and the mill standing still, sells eggs to buy bread.
G1Vedova.2.short: Panna Kovács, the miller's widow, stops you at the market. Her husband died without saying where he hid his savings.

G1Vedova.3.full: "You talk to the dead," she says, without lowering her voice. "The whole village knows it. Madame wants a florin a séance, and I haven't got a florin. You ask him where the money is. He'll answer you: you're educated people."
G1Vedova.3.easy: "You talk to the dead," she says, without lowering her voice. "The whole village knows it. Madame wants a florin a séance, and I haven't got a florin. You ask him where the money is. He'll answer you: you're educated people."
G1Vedova.3.short: "You talk to the dead. Madame wants a florin, and I haven't got one. You ask him where the money is."

G1Vedova.5.full: You improvise a séance and make a guess.

G1Vedova.6.full: You take her to Madame Vámos, and pay yourself.

G1Vedova.7.full: You tell her the truth: you cannot talk to the dead.

G1Vedova.8.full: You take her behind the bread stall, hold her hands and close your eyes, as you have seen Madame do. After what seems a decent interval you say the first thing that comes into your head: behind the stove, a loose brick. The widow kisses your hands and runs to the mill.
G1Vedova.8.easy: You take her behind the bread stall, hold her hands and close your eyes, as you have seen Madame do. After a while you say the first thing that comes into your head: behind the stove, a loose brick. The widow kisses your hands and runs to the mill.
G1Vedova.8.short: You fake a séance and say the first thing that comes to mind: behind the stove, a loose brick. The widow runs to the mill.

G1Vedova.9.full: She comes back in the evening, covered in soot: there was nothing behind the stove. But she is not angry. She says her husband trusted nobody, not even dead, and yet she, for the first time in months, has slept. The next day the village is saying that the family from the estate comforts widows for free.
G1Vedova.9.easy: She comes back in the evening, covered in soot: there was nothing behind the stove. But she is not angry. She says her husband trusted no one, not even dead, but that she, for the first time in months, has slept. The next day the village says the family from the estate comforts widows for free.
G1Vedova.9.short: There was nothing behind the stove. But the widow, for the first time in months, has slept.

G1Vedova.11.full: Madame Vámos accepts your florin without looking at it. The séance is short: the medium is silent for a long time, then speaks in a hoarse voice, a man's, and says to count the paddles of the wheel, from the left, up to the seventh.
G1Vedova.11.easy: Madame Vámos takes your florin without looking at it. The séance is short: the medium is silent for a long time, then speaks in a hoarse man's voice and says to count the paddles of the wheel, from the left, up to the seventh.
G1Vedova.11.short: Madame takes the florin. In a man's voice she says: count the paddles of the wheel to the seventh.

G1Vedova.12.full: Under the seventh paddle, in a tin box wedged between the boards, are the miller's savings, down to the last kreuzer. The widow cries, laughs, swears that from Sunday she will go to the Thursday séances instead of Mass. You wonder how Madame knew; and whether she knew before you paid her.
G1Vedova.12.easy: Under the seventh paddle, in a tin box wedged between the boards, are the miller's savings, down to the last kreuzer. The widow cries, laughs, and swears that from Sunday she will go to the Thursday séances instead of Mass. You wonder how Madame knew; and whether she knew before you paid her.
G1Vedova.12.short: Under the seventh paddle are the savings. You wonder how Madame knew, and since when.

G1Vedova.14.full: You tell her that no, you cannot talk to the dead, and that whoever swears they can usually wants a florin. The widow is silent for a moment. Then she thanks you: in the whole village you are the first person who has promised her nothing.
G1Vedova.14.easy: You tell her that no, you cannot talk to the dead, and that anyone who swears they can usually wants a florin. The widow is silent for a moment. Then she thanks you: in the whole village you are the first person who has promised her nothing.
G1Vedova.14.short: You tell her the truth. She thanks you: you are the first who has promised her nothing.

G1Vedova.15.full: Before leaving she puts her best hen into your arms, struggling and protesting. Refusing it would be an insult; and in the laboratory, as everyone knows, an animal always comes in handy.
G1Vedova.15.easy: Before she goes she puts her best hen into your arms, flapping and protesting. Refusing it would be an insult; and in the laboratory, as everyone knows, an animal always comes in handy.
G1Vedova.15.short: She gives you her best hen. In the laboratory an animal always comes in handy.

G1Stagno.3.full: **TRAGEDY AT THE POND.** On Sunday afternoon little Péter Szűcs, known as Peti, aged eight, the cooper's son, fell through the ice of the park pond, where he was playing with other children despite the prohibition. The body was recovered only yesterday, after three days of searching.
G1Stagno.3.easy: **TRAGEDY AT THE POND.** On Sunday afternoon little Péter Szűcs, called Peti, eight years old, the cooper's son, fell through the ice of the park pond, where he was playing with other children although it was forbidden. The body was found only yesterday, after three days of searching.
G1Stagno.3.short: **TRAGEDY AT THE POND.** Peti, aged eight, the cooper's son, fell through the ice of the pond. He was found after three days.

G1Stagno.4.full: Those who saw him report a singular fact: the boy did not look drowned, but asleep, with rosy cheeks and lips slightly parted. The doctor attributed this to the cold. The mother refuses to have him buried. Madame Vámos has offered to watch over him for a whole night. The cooper, it is said, has debts, and the family from the estate buys bodies for its studies.
G1Stagno.4.easy: Those who saw him tell of something strange: the boy did not look drowned, but asleep, with pink cheeks and lips slightly open. The doctor says it was the cold. The mother will not let him be buried. Madame Vámos has offered to watch over him for a whole night. The cooper, they say, has debts, and the family from the estate buys bodies for its studies.
G1Stagno.4.short: Peti looks asleep. His mother will not bury him, Madame wants to watch over him, and the estate buys bodies for its studies.

G1Stagno.6.full: You pay for the funeral and the headstone.

G1Stagno.7.full: You ask for the body for your studies.

G1Stagno.8.full: You let Madame watch over him.

G1Stagno.9.full: You pay for a white coffin, a small headstone with an angel and a meal for the village after the Mass. Father Anzelm celebrates with shining eyes. Peti's mother does not thank you: she speaks to no one. But the next day, on the estate doorstep, you find a basket of apples wrapped in straw, and no note.
G1Stagno.9.easy: You pay for a white coffin, a small headstone with an angel and a meal for the village after the Mass. Father Anzelm says Mass with shining eyes. Peti's mother does not thank you: she speaks to no one. But the next day, on the estate doorstep, you find a basket of apples wrapped in straw, with no note.
G1Stagno.9.short: You pay for Peti's funeral. His mother speaks to no one, but the next day she leaves you a basket of apples.

G1Stagno.11.full: The cooper takes the money without looking you in the face. The body arrives at the estate at night, on a cart covered with sacks. In the laboratory you examine it for a long time, by lamplight: no water in the lungs, no sign of a struggle, the heart stopped like a clock nobody has wound.
G1Stagno.11.easy: The cooper takes the money without looking you in the eye. The body comes to the estate at night, on a cart covered with sacks. In the laboratory you examine it for a long time, by lamplight: no water in the lungs, no sign of a struggle, the heart stopped like a clock no one has wound.
G1Stagno.11.short: The cooper sells the body. In the laboratory you find Peti did not drown: his heart simply stopped.

G1Stagno.12.full: You take notes all night. At dawn, when you look up from the notebook, it seems to you that the child's eyelids have moved. Not yours: his. You close the notebook, and for a month you do not open it again.
G1Stagno.12.easy: You take notes all night. At dawn, when you look up from your notebook, it seems to you that the child's eyelids have moved. Not yours: his. You close the notebook, and do not open it again for a month.
G1Stagno.12.short: At dawn the child's eyelids seem to have moved. You close your notebook for a month.

G1Stagno.14.full: Madame Vámos watches over the child in the cooper's workshop, among the staves and iron hoops, with a single candle. You stay on the threshold, because someone from the family must be there: she asked for it specifically.
G1Stagno.14.easy: Madame Vámos watches over the child in the cooper's workshop, among the staves and iron hoops, with one candle. You stay in the doorway, because someone from the family must be there: she asked for it.
G1Stagno.14.short: Madame watches over the child. You stay in the doorway: she wanted someone from the family.

G1Stagno.15.full: Towards three the medium bends over the little body, speaks into its ear, listens. Then she turns to the mother and tells her that Peti is cold, but not afraid, and that he will play with the other children again, when the fog comes. The next day they bury him. At the funeral the mother smiles.
G1Stagno.15.easy: Around three the medium bends over the small body, speaks into its ear, and listens. Then she turns to the mother and tells her that Peti is cold, but not afraid, and that he will play with the other children again, when the fog comes. The next day they bury him. At the funeral the mother smiles.
G1Stagno.15.short: Madame tells the mother that Peti will play with the other children again, when the fog comes. At the funeral the mother smiles.

G1Terreno.2.full: At the Builder's Office a young clerk is waiting for you, with a black carnation in his buttonhole and a leather folder under his arm. He represents, he says, "a society of well-to-do and discreet people" who wish to buy your family's strip of land between the cemetery and the high road: a field of nettles where the gravedigger's goats graze.
G1Terreno.2.easy: At the Builder's Office a young clerk is waiting for you, with a black carnation in his buttonhole and a leather folder under his arm. He represents, he says, "a society of wealthy and discreet people" who want to buy your family's strip of land between the cemetery and the main road: a field of nettles where the gravedigger's goats graze.
G1Terreno.2.short: A young man with a black carnation wants to buy your field by the cemetery.

G1Terreno.3.full: The price he offers is twice what it is worth, and three times what anyone in {0} has ever paid for a field of nettles. The foreman, behind him, signals to you with his whole face to accept.
G1Terreno.3.easy: He offers twice what it is worth, and three times what anyone in {0} has ever paid for a field of nettles. The foreman, behind him, signals with his whole face for you to accept.
G1Terreno.3.short: He offers twice what it is worth. The foreman signals you to accept.

G1Terreno.6.full: You refuse: the family's land is not for sale.

G1Terreno.7.full: You ask what they want to build there.

G1Terreno.8.full: You sign, and the young man pays you in gold coins, counted one by one onto a black silk handkerchief. The gravedigger's goats are moved the next day. For years nothing is built on the field; but every now and then, at night, someone walks there with a lantern, pacing out the distance from the graves.
G1Terreno.8.easy: You sign, and the young man pays you in gold coins, counted one by one onto a black silk handkerchief. The gravedigger's goats are moved the next day. For years nothing is built on the field; but now and then, at night, someone walks there with a lantern, pacing out the distance from the graves.
G1Terreno.8.short: You sell. For years nothing is built, but at night someone paces out the field.

G1Terreno.10.full: The young man does not insist. He puts away his folder, wishes you good day and leaves. A week later the society buys the land next to it, on the other side of the cemetery, at the price of a field of nettles. The foreman looks at you the way one looks at someone who has turned down a dowry.
G1Terreno.10.easy: The young man does not insist. He puts his folder away, wishes you good day and leaves. A week later the society buys the land on the other side of the cemetery, at the price of a field of nettles. The foreman looks at you as if you had turned down a dowry.
G1Terreno.10.short: You refuse. The society buys the land on the other side of the cemetery.

G1Terreno.12.full: The young man hesitates, then opens the folder and shows you a drawing: a low, elegant building, with a bell tower without a bell; and from the tower run dozens of thin wires, taut as harp strings, going down to the graves of the cemetery, one by one. "A house of rest," he says. "For the living, of course."
G1Terreno.12.easy: The young man hesitates, then opens the folder and shows you a drawing: a low, elegant building with a bell tower but no bell; from the tower dozens of thin wires run down, taut as harp strings, to the graves, one by one. "A house of rest," he says. "For the living, of course."
G1Terreno.12.short: The drawing shows a building with a bell tower but no bell, and many wires stretched to the graves.

G1Terreno.13.full: You do not sell. But at home you copy the drawing from memory, and redo it three times before you understand what the wires are for.
G1Terreno.13.easy: You do not sell. But at home you copy the drawing from memory, and draw it three times before you understand what the wires are for.
G1Terreno.13.short: You do not sell. At home you copy the drawing, and work out what the wires are for.

G1Chiavi.2.full: The smith takes you aside, near the forge, with the air of someone getting something off his chest. Last summer, shortly before Father died, an elegant gentleman with a black carnation in his buttonhole ordered from him copies of all the keys to the estate: the gate, the front door, the study, the cellar, even the writing desk. He brought him the wax moulds already made.
G1Chiavi.2.easy: The smith takes you aside, near the forge, like someone getting something off his chest. Last summer, just before Father died, an elegant gentleman with a black carnation ordered copies of all the estate's keys from him: the gate, the front door, the study, the cellar, even the writing desk. He brought the wax moulds ready-made.
G1Chiavi.2.short: Before Father died, a gentleman with a black carnation had copies made of all the estate's keys.

G1Chiavi.3.full: "The strange thing," says the smith, lowering his voice, "is that the moulds were brought to me by your father himself, the day before. He put them in my hand and said: when a gentleman with a black flower comes to collect them, give them to him. It is all paid for."
G1Chiavi.3.easy: "The strange thing," says the smith quietly, "is that the moulds were brought to me by your father himself, the day before. He put them in my hand and said: when a gentleman with a black flower comes for them, give them to him. It is all paid for."
G1Chiavi.3.short: "Your father brought me the moulds himself," says the smith. "He said to give them to the gentleman with the black flower."

G1Chiavi.4.full: Behind the forge, Jóska is listening to everything wide-eyed, and gives you a nod, as between accomplices.
G1Chiavi.4.easy: Behind the forge, Jóska listens to it all wide-eyed, and gives you a nod, as between partners in crime.
G1Chiavi.4.short: Jóska hears it all, and gives you a knowing nod.

G1Chiavi.6.full: You have all the locks of the estate changed.

G1Chiavi.7.full: You have a copy made for yourself: the key to the Circle's house.

G1Chiavi.8.full: You leave everything as it is: it was your father's wish.

G1Chiavi.9.full: The smith changes all the locks in a week, and for a few nights the estate seems quieter. Then one morning you find the study door open, the new key in the lock on the inside, and the Journal on the desk open at the last page, the one with the sentence underlined twice.
G1Chiavi.9.easy: The smith changes all the locks in a week, and for a few nights the estate seems quieter. Then one morning you find the study door open, the new key in the lock from the inside, and the Journal on the desk open at the last page, the one with the sentence underlined twice.
G1Chiavi.9.short: You change the locks. But one morning the study is open from the inside, and the Journal lies open at the last page.

G1Chiavi.10.full: If you can, pay $2: gain 2VP. Otherwise gain 1VP.

G1Chiavi.11.full: The smith keeps the moulds of all his customers, the Circle's too. For a few coins he makes you a copy: a long, dark key, with an eye cut into the handle. It opens a door at the back of the house on the square. One night you use it: behind the door there is a staircase, a cellar and, against the wall, a padded little hammer hanging from a rope.
G1Chiavi.11.easy: The smith keeps the moulds of all his customers, the Circle's too. For a few coins he makes you a copy: a long, dark key with an eye cut into the handle. It opens a door at the back of the house on the square. One night you use it: behind the door are some stairs, a cellar and, against the wall, a padded little hammer hanging from a rope.
G1Chiavi.11.short: With the copied key you get into the Circle's cellar at night. Against the wall hangs a padded little hammer on a rope.

G1Chiavi.13.full: You leave things as they are. The gentleman with the carnation never comes, at least not by day. But one night you hear the gate opening, the front door opening, the study door opening, one after another, unhurried, with the right keys. In the morning nothing is missing. On the desk there is a black carnation.
G1Chiavi.13.easy: You leave things as they are. The gentleman with the carnation never comes, at least not by day. But one night you hear the gate open, then the front door, then the study door, one after another, unhurried, with the right keys. In the morning nothing is missing. On the desk is a black carnation.
G1Chiavi.13.short: One night you hear every door open, one after another. In the morning there is a black carnation on the desk.

G1Lettere.2.full: In the middle years the family begins to receive post the postman never delivered. The letters appear under the door, in the bread basket, once even inside Father's Journal, locked in the writing desk. They are envelopes of heavy paper, with no address and no signature, sealed with black wax; in the wax, an open eye.
G1Lettere.2.easy: In the middle years the family receives letters that the postman never brought. The letters appear under the door, in the bread basket, once even inside Father's Journal, locked in the desk. They are envelopes of heavy paper, with no address and no signature, closed with black wax. In the wax there is the picture of an open eye.
G1Lettere.2.short: Letters arrive that no one delivered, even inside the locked Journal. No address, no signature: only an open eye in black wax.

G1Lettere.3.full: Inside, each time, a few lines in an elegant, old-fashioned hand. The **Circle of the Last Hour** greets the heirs of the great scientist, knows their work, admires their courage and wishes to meet them, one by one, somewhere discreet. They need only present themselves at the address given and speak the right word.
G1Lettere.3.easy: Inside there are always a few lines, in elegant, old-fashioned handwriting. The **Circle of the Last Hour** greets the heirs of the great scientist, knows their work, admires their courage and wants to meet them, one at a time, in a private place. They only need to go to the address given and say the right word.
G1Lettere.3.short: The **Circle of the Last Hour** wishes to meet the heirs, one by one, in secret: go to the address given and say the right word.

G1Lettere.4.full: The family, meanwhile, has begun to withdraw every month the money that arrives from Vienna. Nobody mentions it at table. But from then on the unsigned letters arrive more often, and are more affectionate.
G1Lettere.4.easy: Meanwhile the family has started to collect the money from Vienna every month. No one talks about it at table. But from then on the unsigned letters come more often, and are more affectionate.
G1Lettere.4.short: The family collects the money from Vienna. The unsigned letters come more often, and more fondly.

G1Lettere.5.full: The family, meanwhile, keeps sending back to Vienna the money that arrives every month, and every month the money comes back, doubled. From then on the unsigned letters have an offended tone, like those of a neglected aunt.
G1Lettere.5.easy: Meanwhile the family keeps sending the money back to Vienna each month, and each month it comes back, doubled. From then on the unsigned letters sound offended, like those of a neglected aunt.
G1Lettere.5.short: The family sends the money back, and it returns doubled. The unsigned letters sound offended.

G1Lettere.6.full: At the market, the miller's widow tells anyone willing to listen about the savings found under the seventh paddle, and about who took her to Madame. On Thursdays, at the séances, there is a queue.
G1Lettere.6.easy: At the market, the miller's widow tells anyone who will listen about the savings found under the seventh paddle, and who took her to Madame. On Thursdays there is a queue for the séances.
G1Lettere.6.short: The widow tells everyone about the savings Madame found. There is a queue for the Thursday séances.

G1Lettere.7.full: At the market, the miller's widow tells anyone willing to listen about the séance behind the bread stall. She found nothing, she says; but for the first time she slept. In the village people begin to say that the family from the estate comforts better than the priest.
G1Lettere.7.easy: At the market, the miller's widow tells anyone who will listen about the séance behind the bread stall. She found nothing, she says; but for the first time she slept. In the village they begin to say that the family from the estate comforts people better than the priest.
G1Lettere.7.short: The widow says she found nothing, but slept. The village says you comfort people better than the priest.

G1Lettere.8.full: At night, from the cooper's workshop, crying can be heard. In the village they say the family from the estate has bought a dead child and keeps him in a glass case. It is not true; but it is not entirely false either.
G1Lettere.8.easy: At night, crying can be heard from the cooper's workshop. In the village they say the family from the estate has bought a dead child and keeps him in a glass case. It is not true; but it is not quite false either.
G1Lettere.8.short: At night crying comes from the cooper's. The village says you keep a dead child in a glass case.

G1Lettere.9.full: Peti's mother goes to all the Thursday séances, in the front row, and every now and then laughs to herself.
G1Lettere.9.easy: Peti's mother goes to every Thursday séance, in the front row, and now and then laughs to herself.
G1Lettere.9.short: Peti's mother goes to every séance, and now and then laughs to herself.

G1Lettere.10.full: On the field beside the cemetery, the one the family sold, someone has planted stakes with string, in regular rows, as if for a vegetable garden. Or for another cemetery.
G1Lettere.10.easy: On the field by the cemetery, the one the family sold, someone has driven in stakes with string, in neat rows, as if for a vegetable garden. Or for another cemetery.
G1Lettere.10.short: On the field you sold, someone has set stakes in rows, as for a garden. Or a cemetery.

G1Lettere.11.full: What do you do with these letters?

G1Lettere.12.full: You answer, in writing, leaving the envelope under the door.

G1Lettere.13.full: You burn them without finishing them.

G1Lettere.14.full: The answer is written by whoever in the family has the finest handwriting, on estate paper, in a few courteous and cautious lines. The envelope, left under the door in the evening, is gone in the morning. In its place is a fresh black carnation, with a drop of dew that does not fall.
G1Lettere.14.easy: The reply is written by whoever in the family has the best handwriting, on estate paper, in a few polite and careful lines. The envelope, left under the door in the evening, is gone in the morning. In its place is a fresh black carnation, with a drop of dew that does not fall.
G1Lettere.14.short: You reply in a few careful lines. In the morning, in place of the envelope, is a black carnation.

G1Lettere.16.full: The letters burn well, with a high, cheerful flame, and for a few days no more arrive. Then one morning, in the cold fireplace, among the ashes, there is an envelope intact, with black sealing wax and the open eye. It is not even blackened.
G1Lettere.16.easy: The letters burn well, with a high, cheerful flame, and for a few days no more come. Then one morning, in the cold fireplace, among the ashes, lies an envelope, whole, with black sealing wax and the open eye. It is not even scorched.
G1Lettere.16.short: You burn the letters. But one morning, among the ashes, lies an unburnt envelope.

G1Lettere.18.full: From the **The Cost of Disease** Scenario Box, take the **Letter cards** and keep only the **4** that name the **Builder's Office** or the **Cemetery**. Return the others to the box.

G1Lettere.19.full: Shuffle them and give one face down to each player. Each player reads their own in secret.

G1R3.3.full: Turn to **page 3** of the Village Chronicle, **The Cost of Disease** section ({icon:S1_ScenarioIcon}).

G1R3.23.full: The village will have to decide what to do about the woman in the wagon.

G1Sacrestia.2.full: Father Anzelm is waiting for you on the church steps with his hat in his hand, and that alone is strange enough. He takes you to the old sacristy, the one behind the apse that has not been used since they built the new one, and shows you a low little door of dark wood, shut with a rusty bolt.
G1Sacrestia.2.easy: Father Anzelm is waiting for you on the church steps with his hat in his hand, and that alone is strange enough. He takes you to the old sacristy, behind the apse, which has not been used since they built the new one, and shows you a low little door of dark wood, shut with a rusty bolt.
G1Sacrestia.2.short: Father Anzelm takes you to the old sacristy, to a little door shut with a bolt.

G1Sacrestia.3.full: "For three weeks," he says, "someone has been knocking behind there. At night, during vespers, even during Mass. I opened it: it is an empty cupboard, as big as a confessional. I blessed it: they knock all the same." He passes a hand over his face. "I want it walled up. The mason wants three florins, and the parish has not got them. You, on the other hand, know all about knocking."
G1Sacrestia.3.easy: "For three weeks," he says, "someone has been knocking behind it. At night, at vespers, even during Mass. I opened it: it is an empty cupboard, the size of a confessional. I blessed it: they knock just the same." He rubs a hand over his face. "I want it bricked up. The mason wants three florins, and the parish has not got them. You, on the other hand, know all about knocking."
G1Sacrestia.3.short: "There has been knocking behind it for three weeks, even during Mass. I want it bricked up, but the parish has no money."

G1Sacrestia.5.full: You pay the mason: the door is to be walled up.

G1Sacrestia.6.full: You ask to open it one last time, first.

G1Sacrestia.7.full: The mason works a whole afternoon, in silence, brick by brick, while the priest says the rosary on the threshold. When the last brick is in place, the knocking stops. Father Anzelm clasps both your hands: it is the first time you have seen him smile.
G1Sacrestia.7.easy: The mason works a whole afternoon, in silence, brick by brick, while the priest says the rosary in the doorway. When the last brick is in place, the knocking stops. Father Anzelm takes both your hands: it is the first time you have seen him smile.
G1Sacrestia.7.short: The door is bricked up, and the knocking stops. For the first time you see Father Anzelm smile.

G1Sacrestia.8.full: As you leave, you look at the wall, fresh with mortar. You have the feeling, which you cannot explain, that one day someone will open it again, and find behind it something that is not there now.
G1Sacrestia.8.easy: As you leave, you look at the fresh mortar. You have the feeling, which you cannot explain, that one day someone will open it again and find behind it something that is not there now.
G1Sacrestia.8.short: You feel that one day someone will open that wall again, and find something that is not there now.

G1Sacrestia.9.full: Gain 1VP and move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track.

G1Sacrestia.10.full: The priest draws back the bolt reluctantly. The cupboard is empty, dusty, smelling of old wax. But the inside of the door, at head height, is covered with knuckle marks: hundreds of little dents in the wood, some old and darkened, others pale as if they were from last night.
G1Sacrestia.10.easy: The priest pulls back the bolt unwillingly. The cupboard is empty and dusty, smelling of old wax. But the inside of the door, at head height, is covered with knuckle marks: hundreds of little dents in the wood, some old and dark, others pale, as if from last night.
G1Sacrestia.10.short: The cupboard is empty. But the inside of the door is covered in knuckle marks, some of them fresh.

G1Sacrestia.11.full: In a corner, under the dust, there is a register bound in parchment: exorcisms performed in that sacristy from 1711 to 1763, with the names, the dates and, in the margin, the number of knocks heard. The priest lets you take it away, as long as you never mention it to him again. The next day the door is walled up all the same.
G1Sacrestia.11.easy: In a corner, under the dust, is a register bound in parchment: the exorcisms performed in that sacristy from 1711 to 1763, with names, dates and, in the margin, the number of knocks heard. The priest lets you take it away, as long as you never speak of it to him again. The next day the door is bricked up anyway.
G1Sacrestia.11.short: There is also an eighteenth-century register of exorcisms, counting the knocks. The priest lets you take it.

G1Sindaco.2.full: Mayor Bódi receives you in his office, a room with a portrait of the emperor, a smoking stove and a cupboard full of files nobody has ever read. He is a fat, courteous man with permanently damp hands, and he knows the price of everything: of cows, of votes, of souls.
G1Sindaco.2.easy: Mayor Bódi receives you in his office, a room with a portrait of the emperor, a smoking stove and a cupboard full of files no one has ever read. He is a fat, polite man with hands that are always damp, and he knows the price of everything: cows, votes, souls.
G1Sindaco.2.short: Mayor Bódi, fat and polite, knows the price of everything: cows, votes, souls.

G1Sindaco.3.full: "The council will have to decide about the lady of the caravan," he says, without your having asked. "The priest has already called on me. And so has a very elegant gentleman, with a flower in his buttonhole. Everyone asks me to speak. Nobody asks me what I need." He sighs. "The family from the estate, at least, are reasonable people."
G1Sindaco.3.easy: "The council will have to decide about the lady of the caravan," he says, though you have not asked. "The priest has already been to see me. And so has a very elegant gentleman, with a flower in his buttonhole. They all ask me to speak. No one asks me what I need." He sighs. "The family from the estate, at least, are reasonable people."
G1Sindaco.3.short: "The priest and a gentleman with a buttonhole flower want me to speak. No one asks what I need."

G1Sindaco.5.full: You offer him money to speak in favour of Madame.

G1Sindaco.6.full: You remind him of his father's debts to yours.

G1Sindaco.7.full: You ask him to speak against the medium.

G1Sindaco.8.full: The Mayor counts the coins on his desk as naturally as one counts sheep. He promises he will speak, and speak well. Then, seeing you to the door, he confides that the gentleman with the flower in his buttonhole had offered him twice as much, "but with you, of course, it's different: you're local people".
G1Sindaco.8.easy: The Mayor counts the coins on the desk as easily as counting sheep. He promises he will speak, and speak well. Then, walking you to the door, he tells you that the gentleman with the flower had offered him twice as much, "but with you, of course, it's different: you're local people".
G1Sindaco.8.short: The Mayor takes the money and promises to speak well. The gentleman with the flower, he admits, offered double.

G1Sindaco.9.full: If you can, pay $2: gain 3VP. Otherwise nothing happens.

G1Sindaco.10.full: You take out of the Journal a yellowed receipt: a loan your father made to old Bódi, thirty years ago, which nobody ever repaid. The Mayor turns pale, then red, then laughs, and the laugh does not reach his eyes.
G1Sindaco.10.easy: You take a yellowed receipt from the Journal: a loan your father made to old Bódi thirty years ago, which no one ever paid back. The Mayor goes pale, then red, then laughs, and the laugh does not reach his eyes.
G1Sindaco.10.short: You show him an old receipt: a loan never repaid. The Mayor laughs, but not with his eyes.

G1Sindaco.11.full: "I'll speak as you wish," he says. "But the Bódis have long memories. My son will have it, and my son's son." You leave with the receipt in your pocket and the feeling of having made a very bad bargain.
G1Sindaco.11.easy: "I will speak as you like," he says. "But the Bódis have long memories. My son will have it, and my son's son." You leave with the receipt in your pocket and the feeling that you have made a very bad deal.
G1Sindaco.11.short: "I will speak as you like. But the Bódis have long memories." It feels like a very bad deal.

G1Sindaco.13.full: The Mayor listens, nods, agrees with you about everything. He will speak against the medium, he says, because the village needs order and Masses, not little tables. He asks nothing in return, and that makes you more suspicious than any request.
G1Sindaco.13.easy: The Mayor listens, nods, agrees with you on everything. He will speak against the medium, he says, because the village needs order and Masses, not little tables. He asks for nothing in return, and that makes you more suspicious than any demand.
G1Sindaco.13.short: The Mayor will speak against the medium, and asks for nothing. That makes you suspicious.

G1Sindaco.14.full: Two days later you learn that the parish has let him off the rent on a field for ten years. Father Anzelm, when you meet him, greets you as one greets an ally.
G1Sindaco.14.easy: Two days later you learn that the parish has let him off the rent on a field for ten years. Father Anzelm, when you meet him, greets you like an ally.
G1Sindaco.14.short: Then you learn the parish has waived a rent for him. Father Anzelm greets you like an ally.

G1Studente.2.full: Among the stalls of the Farmer's Market there is a young man in a threadbare coat, with round spectacles and a notebook open on his palm. His name is Béla Lukács, the village doctor's nephew: he studies medicine in Vienna and spends the summer in the village taking notes on everything, from the diseases of cows to the miracles of the lady of the caravan.
G1Studente.2.easy: Among the stalls of the Farmer's Market is a young man in a worn coat, with round glasses and a notebook open in his hand. His name is Béla Lukács, the village doctor's nephew: he studies medicine in Vienna and spends the summer in the village taking notes on everything, from the diseases of cows to the miracles of the lady of the caravan.
G1Studente.2.short: At the market is Béla Lukács, the doctor's nephew: he studies medicine in Vienna and takes notes on everything.

G1Studente.3.full: "I don't believe in ghosts," he tells you, before he has even introduced himself. "I believe in experiments. I've prepared a sealed envelope with a number inside: only I know it. If Madame Vámos reads it without opening it, I'll be converted. But she won't let me into the caravan." He holds out the envelope. "You, on the other hand, she will."
G1Studente.3.easy: "I don't believe in ghosts," he says, before he has even introduced himself. "I believe in experiments. I have prepared a sealed envelope with a number inside: only I know it. If Madame Vámos reads it without opening it, I will be converted. But she won't let me into the caravan." He hands you the envelope. "You, on the other hand, she will."
G1Studente.3.short: "I don't believe in ghosts. If Madame reads the number in this envelope without opening it, I'll be converted. You take it: she won't let me in."

G1Studente.5.full: You help him: you take the envelope to the séance.

G1Studente.7.full: At the séance you put the envelope on the table. Madame barely brushes it with her fingertips, closes her eyes and says: "Forty-seven." The next day young Lukács opens the envelope in front of you. It says forty-seven.
G1Studente.7.easy: At the séance you put the envelope on the table. Madame barely touches it with her fingertips, closes her eyes and says: "Forty-seven." The next day young Lukács opens the envelope in front of you. It says forty-seven.
G1Studente.7.short: Madame touches the envelope and says: "Forty-seven." The envelope says exactly that.

G1Studente.8.full: He is not converted, though. He takes the envelope, holds it against the window light, scratches the seal with his fingernail. "Steam," he says, showing you a shadow along the edge of the wax. "Someone opened it and closed it again. I don't know when, or how. But I'll find out." He takes his leave with a little bow: he has found, he says, the first reasonable person in the village.
G1Studente.8.easy: But he is not converted. He holds the envelope against the window light and scratches the seal with his nail. "Steam," he says, showing you a shadow along the edge of the wax. "Someone opened it and closed it again. I don't know when, or how. But I'll find out." He says goodbye with a small bow: he has found, he says, the first reasonable person in the village.
G1Studente.8.short: "Steam," says Lukács. "Someone opened it and closed it again. I'll find out." You are, he says, the first reasonable person in the village.

G1Studente.10.full: You laugh in his face: in a family of scientists, a student with an envelope is an amateur. Young Lukács blushes to the ears, puts the envelope back in his pocket and leaves without saying goodbye.
G1Studente.10.easy: You laugh in his face: in a family of scientists, a student with an envelope is an amateur. Young Lukács goes red to the ears, puts the envelope back in his pocket and leaves without a word.
G1Studente.10.short: You laugh in his face. Lukács goes red and leaves without a word.

G1Studente.11.full: Someone at the market laughs with you. He turns round just once, from the street corner, and looks at you the way one looks at a problem to be solved.
G1Studente.11.easy: Someone at the market laughs with you. He turns round only once, at the corner, and looks at you the way one looks at a problem to be solved.
G1Studente.11.short: He turns round once, and looks at you like a problem to be solved.

G1Lezione.2.full: Madame Vámos's caravan has not moved for eight years: the wheels have sunk into the mud, grass has grown on the roof and the velvet curtains have taken on the colour of rust. Madame lets you in, serves you black tea in a chipped cup and studies you with her head tilted, the way one looks at a horse before buying it.
G1Lezione.2.easy: Madame Vámos's caravan has not moved in eight years: the wheels have sunk into the mud, grass grows on the roof and the velvet curtains have turned the colour of rust. Madame lets you in, gives you black tea in a chipped cup and studies you with her head on one side, the way one looks at a horse before buying it.
G1Lezione.2.short: Madame's caravan has not moved in eight years. She gives you tea and studies you like a horse to buy.

G1Lezione.3.full: "You have the ear," she says. "Your father had it too, but he used it for talking. I can teach you to listen. I am not asking for money." She smiles. "With your family, money comes later."
G1Lezione.3.easy: "You have the ear," she says. "Your father had it too, but he used it for talking. I can teach you to listen. I'm not asking for money." She smiles. "With your family, money comes later."
G1Lezione.3.short: "You have the ear. I can teach you to listen. With your family, money comes later."

G1Lezione.6.full: You accept, but to find out her tricks.

G1Lezione.8.full: The lessons last all winter, on Thursday evenings. Madame teaches you to breathe slowly, to count the knocks, to leave your hands on the table without pushing. She also teaches you the tricks, the pedal, the thread, the throat voice, and she does it with the same seriousness as the rest. "Tricks are for the days when they don't answer," she says. "But one day they will answer you. Then you won't need me."

She also teaches you the tricks, the pedal, the thread, the throat voice, just as seriously as the rest. "Tricks are for the days when they don't answer," she says. "But one day they will answer you. Then you won't need me."

G1Lezione.10.full: Madame understands at once the real reason for your visits, and is not offended. On the contrary, she teaches you the tricks with a craftswoman's pride: the pedal, the silk thread, phosphorus dissolved in oil, the voice that comes out of the throat without moving the lips. You write them all down, in a notebook.
G1Lezione.10.easy: Madame understands at once why you really come, and is not offended. In fact she teaches you the tricks with a craftswoman's pride: the pedal, the silk thread, phosphorus dissolved in oil, the voice that comes out of the throat without moving the lips. You write them all down in a notebook.
G1Lezione.10.short: Madame knows why you come, and teaches you the tricks with pride. You write them all down.

G1Lezione.11.full: At the last lesson, as you close the notebook, she tells you one thing only: "Tricks are the easy part. The hard part is to stop using them when they are no longer needed."
G1Lezione.11.easy: At the last lesson, as you close the notebook, she tells you just one thing: "Tricks are the easy part. The hard part is to stop using them when they are no longer needed."
G1Lezione.11.short: "Tricks are the easy part. The hard part is stopping when they are no longer needed."

G1Lezione.13.full: You put down your cup and stand up. Madame does not hold you back. "As you wish," she says, showing you to the caravan door. "It doesn't matter. One of your children will come, or one of your children's children. Your blood always comes back." On the threshold she puts a spiced biscuit in your hand, as one does with children.

G1Panchina.2.full: In the Park, near the pond, there is a cast-iron bench with a small brass plate: *Gift of the family of the estate, 1840*. Every evening, at sunset, an old woman sits there with a grey shawl and a basket on her knees, and looks towards the hill. Someone tells you she was Father's nurse, in his last year.
G1Panchina.2.easy: In the Park, near the pond, there is a cast-iron bench with a small brass plate: *Gift of the family of the estate, 1840*. Every evening at sunset an old woman sits there with a grey shawl and a basket on her knees, looking towards the hill. Someone tells you she was Father's nurse, in his last year.
G1Panchina.2.short: Every evening, on the bench your family gave, sits Father's nurse, looking at the hill.

G1Panchina.3.full: When you sit down beside her she is not surprised. "You have his eyes," she says. "He didn't want to die in bed. He wanted to die sitting up, in the chair beside it, with his eyes open. He said that way he would see her arrive."
G1Panchina.3.easy: When you sit beside her she is not surprised. "You have his eyes," she says. "He didn't want to die in bed. He wanted to die sitting up, in the chair beside it, with his eyes open. He said that way he would see her coming."
G1Panchina.3.short: "You have his eyes. He wanted to die sitting up, eyes open, to see her coming."

G1Panchina.5.full: You ask her about his last hours.

G1Panchina.6.full: You leave her some money: she has little to live on.

G1Panchina.7.full: You have the little plate removed from the bench.

G1Panchina.8.full: The old woman tells it unhurriedly: the fever, the delirium, the formulas spoken aloud like prayers. At the end, she says, Father grew calm, looked at the door and said, clearly: *"Here I am. Punctual as always."* Then he knocked once, with his knuckle, on the arm of the chair. "And someone answered," says the old woman, looking at the hill. "I was there."
G1Panchina.8.easy: The old woman tells it slowly: the fever, the delirium, the formulas said aloud like prayers. At the end, she says, Father grew calm, looked at the door and said clearly: *"Here I am. Punctual as always."* Then he knocked once, with his knuckle, on the arm of the chair. "And someone answered," says the old woman, looking at the hill. "I was there."
G1Panchina.8.short: At the end Father said: *"Here I am. Punctual as always."* He knocked once. "And someone answered," says the old woman. "I was there."

G1Panchina.10.full: The old woman takes the money, counts it and puts it in the basket under a handkerchief. She thanks you as one thanks a relative. From that day on, every week, a jar of blackberry jam appears on the estate doorstep, with a note in capital letters: *"For the eyes."*
G1Panchina.10.easy: The old woman takes the money, counts it and puts it in her basket under a handkerchief. She thanks you as one thanks a relative. From that day, every week, a jar of blackberry jam appears on the estate doorstep, with a note in capitals: *"For the eyes."*
G1Panchina.10.short: Every week a jar of jam appears on your doorstep: *"For the eyes."*

G1Panchina.12.full: The smith unscrews the plate in an afternoon. The bench stays, anonymous, and the old woman goes on sitting there every evening, but looks the other way, towards the village. A week later, in place of the plate, someone has carved two initials with a knife: one is Father's. The other is an E.
G1Panchina.12.easy: The smith unscrews the plate in an afternoon. The bench stays, nameless, and the old woman still sits there every evening, but looks the other way, towards the village. G1Panchina.12.short: You remove the plate. A week later two initials are carved in its place: Father's, and an E.

G1Patto.4.full: A tall man is waiting for you, in a coat too elegant for {0}, with a black carnation in his buttonhole. He does not ask who you are. He calls you by name, offers you his arm and walks with you, slowly, as old friends do.
G1Patto.4.easy: A tall man is waiting for you, with a coat too elegant for {0} and a black carnation in his buttonhole. He does not ask who you are. He calls you by name, gives you his arm and walks with you, slowly, as old friends do.
G1Patto.4.short: A tall man with a black carnation awaits you. He knows your name and walks with you like an old friend.

G1Patto.5.full: "The Circle of the Last Hour," he says, "is a small society of people who will not resign themselves. We have all lost someone; and we have all discovered that the dead are not as far away as the priests say. Madame Vámos is our voice. Your father was… let us say a correspondent."
G1Patto.5.easy: "The Circle of the Last Hour," he says, "is a small group of people who will not resign themselves. We have all lost someone, and we have all found out that the dead are not as far away as the priests say. Madame Vámos is our voice. Your father was… let us say a correspondent."
G1Patto.5.short: "We are people who will not resign ourselves: the dead are not as far as the priests say. Madame Vámos is our voice. Your father was… a correspondent."

G1Patto.6.full: He hands you an envelope, swollen with pages. "Here are things he knew and had no time to teach you. They are yours. In return we ask only a promise: that one day, when the Circle asks you, you will open the door."
G1Patto.6.easy: He gives you an envelope full of pages. "Here are things he knew and did not have time to teach you. They are yours. In return we want only a promise: that one day, when the Circle asks you, you will open the door."
G1Patto.6.short: He hands you an envelope: "What your father knew. In return, a promise: when the Circle asks, you will open the door."

G1Patto.7.full: He does not say which door. He smiles as if you already knew.

G1Patto.10.full: You shake the man's hand. It is as cold as Madame's, and in yours it does not warm. "The Circle thanks you," he says, and walks away without turning round.
G1Patto.10.easy: You shake the man's hand. It is as cold as Madame's and it does not get warm in yours. "The Circle thanks you," he says, and leaves without turning round.
G1Patto.10.short: His hand is as cold as Madame's. "The Circle thanks you."

G1Patto.11.full: The envelope weighs more than it should. That evening, reading it by lamplight, you notice that some of the pages are written in your father's hand, and that one of them is dated two weeks after his death.
G1Patto.11.easy: The envelope is heavier than it should be. That evening you read it by the light of the lamp and see that some pages are written by your father. One of them has a date two weeks after his death.
G1Patto.11.short: The envelope holds pages in your father's hand. One is dated two weeks after his death.

G1Patto.13.full: You hand back the envelope unopened. The man takes no offence; if anything, he seems almost pleased, like someone who has won a small bet with himself. "Refusal is also a form of attention," he says. "We shall meet again." He presses a few coins into your hand "for the trouble" and walks away.
G1Patto.13.easy: You give the envelope back without opening it. The man is not offended. In fact, he seems almost happy, like someone who has won a small bet with himself. G1Patto.13.short: You return the envelope unopened. The man seems almost pleased. "We shall meet again." He leaves you a few coins and goes.

G1Patto.14.full: The next day, at the Cemetery, there is a black carnation on your father's grave. The earth around the headstone has been disturbed, as if someone had pressed an ear to it to listen.
G1Patto.14.easy: The next day, at the Cemetery, there is a black carnation on your father's grave. The earth around the headstone has been moved, as if someone had put an ear to it to listen.
G1Patto.14.short: The next day there is a black carnation on your father's grave, and the earth has been disturbed.

G1Fine.3.full: The council meets in the room above the inn, because the town hall roof leaks. Present are Mayor Bódi, the notary, three landowners, the schoolmaster and, on a chair of his own, Father Anzelm, who has no vote but does have the right to speak, and exercises it for an hour and a half.
G1Fine.3.easy: The council meets in the room above the inn, because rain comes into the town hall. There are Mayor Bódi, the notary, three landowners, the schoolmaster and, on a separate chair, Father Anzelm. He cannot vote but he can speak, and he speaks for an hour and a half.
G1Fine.3.short: The council meets above the inn. Father Anzelm has no vote, but speaks for an hour and a half.

G1Fine.4.full: There is only one item on the agenda: whether Mrs Eszter Vámos, by profession a "consoler", may remain in {0}. In eight years her wagon has become a house with its shutters always closed; her parlour, every Thursday, fills with people who go in weeping and come out smiling; and the Circle of the Last Hour, which no one admits to attending, has bought two plots beside the cemetery.
G1Fine.4.easy: There is only one question to decide: can Mrs Eszter Vámos, whose job is "consoler", stay in {0}? In eight years her wagon has become a house with the shutters always closed. G1Fine.4.short: The question: may the "consoler" Eszter Vámos stay in {0}? In eight years her parlour has filled with the grieving, and the Circle has bought land beside the cemetery.

G1Fine.5.full: The priest speaks of heresy, of fraud, of grief exploited. The notary speaks of taxes duly paid. The Mayor does not speak: he listens, and counts. In the end it is decided, as is the custom in {0} for thorny matters, to let the village's most important families vote as well. And the most important, by now, is the heirs'.
G1Fine.5.easy: The priest talks about heresy, cheating, and grief used to make money. The notary says she pays her taxes. The Mayor does not speak: he listens and counts. In the end they decide, as {0} always does with difficult questions, to let the most important families of the village vote too. And by now the most important is the heirs' family.
G1Fine.5.short: The priest cries heresy, the notary recalls taxes paid. In the end, as is the custom in {0}, the important families vote too. And the most important is the heirs'.

G1Fine.6.full: To everyone's surprise the doctor's nephew also speaks, young Lukács, back from Vienna with his degree fresh in hand: he tells of a sealed envelope, opened and closed again with steam, and asks the council for an inspection of the caravan. The council thanks him and decides nothing.
G1Fine.6.easy: To everyone's surprise the doctor's nephew speaks too, young Lukács, just back from Vienna with his degree: he tells of a sealed envelope opened and closed again with steam, and asks the council to inspect the caravan. The council thanks him and decides nothing.
G1Fine.6.short: Young Lukács, just qualified, speaks too: he asks for the caravan to be inspected. The council decides nothing.

G1Fine.7.full: Mayor Bódi, against all his habits, takes the floor: he speaks of charity, of comfort for the widowed, of the taxes punctually paid by Mrs Vámos. Nobody has ever heard him speak at such length.
G1Fine.7.easy: Mayor Bódi, quite unlike himself, speaks: of charity, of comfort for the bereaved, of the taxes Mrs Vámos pays on time. No one has ever heard him speak for so long.
G1Fine.7.short: Mayor Bódi, quite unlike himself, speaks at length in favour of Mrs Vámos.

G1Fine.8.easy: Mayor Bódi says little and keeps looking at the family from the estate, like a dog looking at the master who has just beaten it.
G1Fine.8.short: Mayor Bódi says little, and looks at you like a beaten dog.

G1Fine.9.easy: Mayor Bódi, to everyone's surprise, takes the priest's side, and even quotes a verse from Leviticus, reading it from a scrap of paper.

G1Domande.2.full: Madame Vámos stays. That same evening the windows of her house light up one by one, and from the parlour comes the sound of a piano that no one in {0} has ever seen delivered. G1Domande.4.full: The next morning, on the estate door, someone has drawn an open eye in charcoal. The servant washes it three times. After the third, the eye is still there, only a little fainter, as if looking up from under water.

G1Domande.6.full: Goes to say goodbye to Madame Vámos.

G1Domande.8.full: Madame Vámos receives you in her new drawing room, still full of crates, with the piano playing by itself in the next room. She offers you plum brandy, thanks you one by one, and holds each of your hands a moment longer than necessary. "We are neighbours now," she says. "For ever, if you like."

G2Intro.4.full: The village had grown. Where the wooden houses had stood there were half-timbered ones with painted beams, a paved street, a post office, two inns and a doctor. The priest was still Father Anzelm, older and thinner, but no less stubborn. And there was, as one of the new heirs wrote in a letter to a sister, "this thing they call the veil here, as if it were a matter of weather, like the rain or the fog".

The priest was still Father Anzelm, older and thinner, but as stubborn as before. And there was, one of the new heirs writes to a sister, "this thing they call the veil here, as if it were the weather, like the rain or the fog".
