G2Mulino.2.full: At the Builder's Office the foreman unrolls on the table the plan of the new road, the one that will link the square to the telegraph station. It runs right over the Kovács family's old mill, idle for nearly thirty years, with its rotten wheel and its caved-in roof. Next week they are pulling it down.
G2Mulino.2.easy: At the Builder's Office the foreman unrolls the plan of the new road on the table, the one that will link the square to the telegraph station. It runs right over the Kovács family's old mill, idle for almost thirty years, with its rotten wheel and caved-in roof. Next week they are knocking it down.
G2Mulino.2.short: The new road runs over the old Kovács mill. Next week they knock it down.

G2Mulino.3.full: The name rings a bell. In the family they used to tell of a widow, of a séance improvised behind the bread stall, of a brick behind the stove where there was nothing.
G2Mulino.3.easy: The name rings a bell. Your family used to tell of a widow, a séance made up behind the bread stall, and a brick behind the stove with nothing behind it.
G2Mulino.3.short: Your family told of a widow and a brick behind the stove, with nothing behind it.

G2Mulino.4.full: The name rings a bell. In the family they used to tell of a widow, of Madame Vámos, of the seventh paddle of the wheel. The widow, later, left the mill to the Circle; and the Circle is now selling it to the road.
G2Mulino.4.easy: The name rings a bell. Your family used to tell of a widow, of Madame Vámos, of the seventh paddle of the wheel. Later the widow left the mill to the Circle; and now the Circle is selling it for the road.
G2Mulino.4.short: Your family told of the seventh paddle. Later the widow left the mill to the Circle, which is now selling it.

G2Mulino.5.full: The name rings a bell. In the family they used to tell of an honest widow and a hen; and of a miller who trusted nobody, not even when dead.
G2Mulino.5.easy: The name rings a bell. Your family used to tell of an honest widow and a hen; and of a miller who trusted no one, not even dead.
G2Mulino.5.short: Your family told of a miller who trusted no one, not even dead.

G2Mulino.6.full: You, after all, already know what was behind the mill's stove: a private séance, at the Pub, led you to find it. But a miller who trusted nobody, you think, would not have put everything in the same place.
G2Mulino.6.easy: You already know, of course, what was behind the mill stove: a private séance at the Pub led you to it. But a miller who trusted no one, you think, would not have put everything in one place.
G2Mulino.6.short: You already found the box behind the stove. But a miller like that, you think, would not keep everything in one place.

G2Mulino.7.full: "If you want to take a look before the pickaxes arrive," says the foreman, "go ahead. There's nothing left inside. Everybody says so."
G2Mulino.7.easy: "If you want to have a look before the pickaxes come," says the foreman, "go ahead. There's nothing left inside. Everyone says so."
G2Mulino.7.short: "Have a look if you like. There's nothing left inside."

G2Mulino.10.full: You have the widow's heirs told to search it themselves.

G2Mulino.11.full: The stove is a mass of blackened bricks, covered in swallows' nests. The third brick from the bottom moves under your fingers. Behind it there is a rusty tin box, and inside a roll of old coins and a note written in charcoal: *"For my wife. Somebody tell her, because I can't."*
G2Mulino.11.easy: The stove is a heap of blackened bricks, covered in swallows' nests. The third brick from the bottom moves under your fingers. Behind it is a rusty tin box, and inside a roll of old coins and a note written in charcoal: *"For my wife. Someone tell her, because I can't."*
G2Mulino.11.short: Behind the third brick is a box of coins and a note: *"For my wife. Someone tell her, because I can't."*

G2Mulino.12.full: It was behind the stove. It always had been. A fake séance, twenty-five years ago, had told the truth; and nobody had come to look closely enough.
G2Mulino.12.easy: It was behind the stove. It always had been. A fake séance, twenty-five years ago, had told the truth; and no one had looked carefully enough.
G2Mulino.12.short: It was behind the stove. A fake séance, twenty-five years ago, had told the truth.

G2Mulino.13.full: Which means, you think, that the money Madame had them find under the seventh paddle was something else. Who had put it there? And why?
G2Mulino.13.easy: Which means, you think, that the money Madame found for her under the seventh paddle was something else. Who had put it there? And why?
G2Mulino.13.short: So the money under the seventh paddle was something else. Who put it there?

G2Mulino.15.full: You send for the widow Kovács's grandsons, two lads who work as carters, and tell them to search the mill before the pickaxes. They come back in the evening with a tin box, found behind the stove, and with shining eyes. Inside were their grandfather's savings, and a note for their grandmother.
G2Mulino.15.easy: You send for the widow Kovács's grandsons, two young carters, and tell them to search the mill before the pickaxes come. They come back in the evening with a tin box found behind the stove, and tears in their eyes. Inside were their grandfather's savings, and a note for their grandmother.
G2Mulino.15.short: The widow's grandsons find their grandfather's savings behind the stove, and a note for their grandmother.

G2Mulino.16.full: The widow has been dead for years. The young men take the note to the cemetery and bury it beside her, with their own hands. Then they come to the estate to say thank you, caps in hand.
G2Mulino.16.easy: The widow has been dead for years. The young men take the note to the cemetery and bury it beside her with their own hands. Then they come to the estate to thank you, caps in hand.
G2Mulino.16.short: The widow is dead. The young men bury the note beside her, and come to thank you.

G2Fossa.2.full: Father Anzelm is dying, and he knows it. He tells no one: he goes to the cemetery with his stick, every morning, and walks among the graves like a buyer viewing a house. The day he meets you he stops in front of your grandfather's grave, the first of your family, and points with his stick at the patch of grass beside it.
G2Fossa.2.easy: Father Anzelm is dying, and he knows it. He tells no one: every morning he goes to the cemetery with his stick and walks among the graves like someone looking over a house to buy. The day he meets you he stops at your grandfather's grave, the first of your family, and points with his stick at the patch of grass beside it.
G2Fossa.2.short: Father Anzelm is dying. At the cemetery he stops at your grandfather's grave and points to the spot beside it.

G2Fossa.3.full: "This plot is yours," he says. "Your family bought it together with the other one, in 1848. I'd like it." He coughs, for a long time. "To keep an eye on him. Thirty years of sermons, and I never managed to make him keep quiet. Perhaps from close by."
G2Fossa.3.easy: "This plot is yours," he says. "Your family bought it along with the other one, in 1848. I'd like it." He coughs, for a long time. "To keep an eye on him. Thirty years of sermons, and I never managed to make him be quiet. Perhaps from close by."
G2Fossa.3.short: "I'd like to be buried here, beside him. To keep an eye on him. Perhaps from close by I can make him be quiet."

G2Fossa.4.full: Then he adds, almost to himself: "The sacristy wall is holding. But since you paid for it, I sometimes wonder who I had it walled up for."
G2Fossa.4.easy: Then he adds, almost to himself: "The sacristy wall is holding. But since you paid for it, I sometimes wonder who I had it bricked up for."
G2Fossa.4.short: "The sacristy wall is holding. But sometimes I wonder who I had it bricked up for."

G2Fossa.5.full: Then he adds, almost to himself: "The register that someone in your family took away from the sacristy. I hope someone in your house has read it. I never had the courage."
G2Fossa.5.easy: Then he adds, almost to himself: "The register someone in your family took from the sacristy. I hope someone in your house has read it. I never had the courage."
G2Fossa.5.short: "I hope someone has read the register your family took from the sacristy. I never had the courage."

G2Fossa.7.full: You give him the plot next to your grandfather.

G2Fossa.8.full: You refuse: that plot belongs to the family.

G2Fossa.9.full: You ask him what he heard knocking, all these years.

G2Fossa.10.full: The old priest shakes your hand with his dry, warm fingers. He dies in November, and they bury him where he asked, a step from your grandfather, with his head the same way. The whole village is at the funeral, even the widows of the Circle, at the back, veils lowered.
G2Fossa.10.easy: The old priest shakes your hand with his dry, warm fingers. He dies in November, and they bury him where he asked, a step from your grandfather, his head pointing the same way. The whole village comes to the funeral, even the Circle's widows, at the back, veils lowered.
G2Fossa.10.short: Father Anzelm dies in November and is buried beside your grandfather. The whole village comes to the funeral.

G2Fossa.11.full: The night after the funeral, at the estate, nobody knocks. Nor the next night, nor the one after. Then, on the fourth night, the knocking starts again: but there are two rhythms now, one over the other, like two old men arguing.
G2Fossa.11.easy: The night after the funeral, at the estate, no one knocks. Nor the night after, nor the one after that. Then, on the fourth night, the knocking starts again: but now there are two rhythms, one over the other, like two old men arguing.
G2Fossa.11.short: For three nights no one knocks. Then the knocking returns, in two rhythms, like two old men arguing.

G2Fossa.13.full: Father Anzelm nods without taking offence, as if he expected it. "You're right," he says. "Let everyone stay with their own." They bury him in November on the other side of the cemetery, near the wall, with the headstone facing your grandfather's grave.
G2Fossa.13.easy: Father Anzelm nods without taking offence, as if he had expected it. "You're right," he says. "Each to his own." They bury him in November on the other side of the cemetery, by the wall, his headstone turned towards your grandfather's grave.
G2Fossa.13.short: "You're right. Each to his own." They bury him across the cemetery, his headstone turned towards your grandfather.

G2Fossa.14.full: The Circle, having heard of your refusal, sends you a black-edged card with a single word: *Thank you.* You are not quite sure for what.
G2Fossa.14.easy: The Circle, hearing of your refusal, sends you a black-edged card with one word: *Thank you.* You are not sure what for.
G2Fossa.14.short: The Circle sends you a card: *Thank you.* You are not sure what for.

G2Fossa.16.full: The priest looks at you for a long time, leaning on his stick. Then he sits down on your grandfather's headstone, without respect, as one sits on a bench. "Your name," he says. "They knocked it out letter by letter. In the sacristy walls, in the alms box, in the wood of the confessional. I did thirty years of exorcisms, and every time they stopped they started again from the beginning, like a schoolboy revising."
G2Fossa.16.easy: The priest looks at you for a long time, leaning on his stick. Then he sits down on your grandfather's headstone, without respect, as one sits on a bench. "Your name," he says. "They knocked it out letter by letter. In the sacristy walls, in the alms box, in the wood of the confessional. I did thirty years of exorcisms, and every time they stopped they began again from the start, like a schoolboy going over his lessons."
G2Fossa.16.short: "Your name," he says. "For thirty years they knocked it out letter by letter, in the church walls."

G2Fossa.17.full: He gets up, with difficulty. "Keep the plot," he adds. "I've changed my mind. I don't want to be near the one who listens." They bury him in November, on the other side of the cemetery.
G2Fossa.17.easy: He gets up with difficulty. "Keep the plot," he adds. "I've changed my mind. I don't want to be near the one who listens." They bury him in November, on the other side of the cemetery.
G2Fossa.17.short: "Keep the plot. I don't want to be near the one who listens." They bury him far away.

G2Medico.2.full: The village doctor of {0} is now Béla Lukács: a man of fifty with a grey beard, round spectacles and a leather bag he never puts down. He took over from his uncle, and with the post also a certain reputation as a blasphemer, because he says in public that the dead do not come back and that whoever swears to seeing them has a diseased liver.
G2Medico.2.easy: The village doctor of {0} is now Béla Lukács: a man of fifty with a grey beard, round glasses and a leather bag he never lets go of. He took over from his uncle, along with a certain name for blasphemy, because he says in public that the dead do not come back and that anyone who swears they see them has a bad liver.
G2Medico.2.short: The doctor is now Béla Lukács. He says in public that anyone who sees the dead has a bad liver.

G2Medico.3.full: "Your family helped me, once," he tells you, "with a sealed envelope. It was the first reasonable person I met in this village. I hope common sense is hereditary."
G2Medico.3.easy: "Your family helped me once," he says, "with a sealed envelope. It was the first reasonable person I met in this village. I hope common sense runs in families."
G2Medico.3.short: "Your family helped me once. I hope common sense runs in families."

G2Medico.4.full: "Your family laughed in my face, once," he tells you, "at the market, in front of everyone. I was twenty-seven. Let's see if you laugh too."
G2Medico.4.easy: "Your family laughed in my face once," he says, "at the market, in front of everyone. I was twenty-seven. Let's see if you laugh too."
G2Medico.4.short: "Your family laughed in my face once. Let's see if you laugh too."

G2Medico.5.full: On the table in the council chamber there is a petition: the doctor asks the Mayor for permission to inspect the places where séances are held "for reasons of hygiene", and to seize anything suspicious he finds there: phosphorus, gauze, threads, bells. The signatures of the notable families are missing.
G2Medico.5.easy: On the council table there is a petition: the doctor asks the Mayor for permission to inspect the places where séances are held "for reasons of hygiene", and to seize anything suspicious he finds: phosphorus, gauze, threads, bells. The signatures of the important families are missing.
G2Medico.5.short: The doctor wants to inspect the séance rooms. The important families have not signed.

G2Medico.8.full: You tell him séances are none of his business.

G2Medico.9.full: Yours is the first signature, and the largest. The inspection takes place on a rainy Tuesday, with two gendarmes and the doctor at their head: phosphorus in a cupboard, rolls of gauze, a bell with a wire disappearing into the ceiling. The Circle says they are cleaning implements. The village laughs for a week, and then forgets.
G2Medico.9.easy: Yours is the first signature, and the biggest. The inspection takes place on a rainy Tuesday, with two gendarmes and the doctor in the lead: phosphorus in a cupboard, rolls of gauze, a bell with a wire disappearing into the ceiling. The Circle says these are for cleaning. The village laughs for a week, and then forgets.
G2Medico.9.short: You sign first. The inspection finds phosphorus, gauze and wires. The village laughs for a week, then forgets.

G2Medico.10.full: Lukács does not. He thanks you, prescribes you free of charge a sleeping draught that works, and from that day greets you in the street as one greets a colleague.
G2Medico.10.easy: Lukács does not. He thanks you, prescribes you a sleeping draught that works, free of charge, and from that day greets you in the street like a colleague.
G2Medico.10.short: Lukács does not: he gives you a sleeping draught that works, and greets you like a colleague.

G2Medico.12.full: The doctor takes off his spectacles, cleans them with his handkerchief and puts them back on very calmly. "I understand," he says. "It runs in the family." The petition stays on the table without your signatures, and the Mayor puts it in a drawer.
G2Medico.12.easy: The doctor takes off his glasses, cleans them with his handkerchief and puts them back on very calmly. "I see," he says. "It runs in the family." The petition stays on the table without your signatures, and the Mayor puts it in a drawer.
G2Medico.12.short: "I see," says the doctor. "It runs in the family." The petition ends up in a drawer.

G2Medico.13.full: Two days later, on the estate doorstep, you find a black carnation and an envelope with some money, without a note. The Circle knows how to be grateful.
G2Medico.13.easy: Two days later, on the estate doorstep, you find a black carnation and an envelope of money, with no note. The Circle knows how to show its gratitude.
G2Medico.13.short: On the doorstep you find a black carnation and some money. The Circle knows how to be grateful.

G2Becchini.2.full: At the Laborer's Union there is an unusual meeting: six gravediggers from the district, caps in hand and with the faces of men who have not slept for weeks. Old Mihály, the village gravedigger, speaks for them all. They will no longer bury after sunset, and they will no longer nail the coffins shut, because for some time now, when they lower a coffin into the grave, someone knocks from inside.
G2Becchini.2.easy: At the Laborer's Union there is an unusual meeting: six gravediggers from the district, caps in hand, with the faces of men who have not slept for weeks. Old Mihály, the village gravedigger, speaks for all of them. They will no longer bury anyone after sunset, and they will no longer nail coffins shut, because for some time now, when they lower a coffin into the grave, someone knocks from inside.
G2Becchini.2.short: The gravediggers will not bury after sunset any more: when they lower a coffin, someone knocks.

G2Becchini.3.full: "Not the new dead," Mihály explains. "The old ones, in the graves alongside. They knock to greet the new ones." Until the estate does something about it, he adds, the district's cemeteries will stay closed in the evening.
G2Becchini.3.easy: "Not the new dead," Mihály explains. "The old ones, in the graves next door. They knock to greet the newcomers." Until the estate does something about it, he adds, the district's cemeteries will stay closed in the evening.
G2Becchini.3.short: "The old dead knock, to greet the new." Until the estate does something, the cemeteries stay closed at night.

G2Becchini.5.full: You pay the gravediggers double wages.

G2Becchini.6.full: You dig yourself, with whoever in the family has the courage to come.

G2Becchini.7.full: You ask the priest to bless the spades.

G2Becchini.8.full: The gravediggers accept the money and go back to work, but only by day, and only three to a grave: one digs, one holds the lantern, one prays. Mihály thanks you with a nod. Burials in {0} become very quick indeed.
G2Becchini.8.easy: The gravediggers take the money and go back to work, but only by day, and only three to a grave: one digs, one holds the lantern, one prays. Mihály thanks you with a nod. Burials in {0} become very quick indeed.
G2Becchini.8.short: Paid, the gravediggers go back to work, but only by day and three to a grave: one digs, one holds the light, one prays.

G2Becchini.10.full: You dig yourself, at night, with your grandfather's spade and a dark lantern. The earth is soft and cold. When the day's coffin reaches the bottom, from the grave alongside comes one knock, then another, polite, like someone knocking at a new neighbour's door. You answer with the spade handle. Afterwards, for some reason, you feel like a guest in someone else's house.
G2Becchini.10.easy: You dig yourself, at night, with your grandfather's spade and a dark lantern. The earth is soft and cold. When the coffin reaches the bottom, from the grave next door comes one knock, then another, polite, like someone knocking at a new neighbour's door. You answer with the spade handle. Afterwards, for some reason, you feel like a guest in someone else's house.
G2Becchini.10.short: You dig at night. From the next grave comes polite knocking, as if greeting a new neighbour. You answer with the spade.

G2Becchini.11.full: The next morning, Mihály offers you a favour of the trade, as his father did with your family.
G2Becchini.11.easy: The next morning Mihály offers you a favour of the trade, as his father did for your family.
G2Becchini.11.short: Mihály offers you a favour of the trade, as his father did for your family.

G2Becchini.13.full: The priest blesses the spades, ropes and lanterns of all the gravediggers in the district, in a short and slightly ridiculous ceremony in the presbytery courtyard. It works, or so it seems: all winter, in the cemeteries, nobody knocks. The gravediggers go back to work, and the priest, for the first time in years, invites you to lunch.
G2Becchini.13.easy: The priest blesses the spades, ropes and lanterns of every gravedigger in the district, in a short and slightly silly ceremony in the presbytery yard. It works, or so it seems: all winter, in the cemeteries, no one knocks. The gravediggers go back to work, and the priest, for the first time in years, invites you to lunch.
G2Becchini.13.short: The priest blesses the spades. All winter no one knocks, and the priest invites you to lunch.

G2Mano.2.full: The village fortune teller is a fat, cheerful woman, with rings on all her fingers and a moth-eaten parrot on a perch. For two coins she reads anyone's palm, and usually says kind things. When she takes yours, though, she stops smiling.
G2Mano.2.easy: The village fortune teller is a fat, cheerful woman, with rings on every finger and a scruffy parrot on a perch. For two coins she reads anyone's palm, and usually says nice things. When she takes yours, though, she stops smiling.
G2Mano.2.short: The fortune teller reads everyone's palm and always says nice things. But when she takes yours, she stops smiling.

G2Mano.3.full: "You have two lifelines," she says, tracing them with her fingernail. "One is yours. The other begins before you were born, and does not end. I have never seen it on anyone. That is: I saw it once, on a gentleman from the estate, many years ago, when I was a girl."
G2Mano.3.easy: "You have two lifelines," she says, tracing them with her nail. "One is yours. The other begins before you were born, and doesn't end. I've never seen it on anyone. Well: I saw it once, on a gentleman from the estate, long ago, when I was a girl."
G2Mano.3.short: "You have two lifelines. One is yours. The other starts before you and never ends. I've only seen it on a gentleman from the estate, long ago."

G2Mano.5.full: You ask her what it means.

G2Mano.6.full: You pay her double not to tell anyone.

G2Mano.7.full: You read her palm yourself, to see how she does it.

G2Mano.8.full: The fortune teller hesitates, then speaks softly, so the parrot will not hear. "It means someone lives in you too," she says. "Someone who hasn't finished. You are his hand, when he wants to write." She closes your fingers into a fist, gently, the way one folds a letter. She will not be paid.
G2Mano.8.easy: The fortune teller hesitates, then speaks quietly, so the parrot won't hear. "It means someone lives in you too," she says. "Someone who hasn't finished. You are his hand, when he wants to write." She folds your fingers into a fist, gently, the way one folds a letter. She will not take money.
G2Mano.8.short: "Someone lives in you too. Someone who hasn't finished. You are his hand, when he wants to write."

G2Mano.10.full: The fortune teller pockets the coins and swears on the parrot that she will tell nobody. The parrot, which heard everything, that same evening repeats at the market, in the fortune teller's voice, *"two lines, two lines"*, until someone throws a cloth over it.
G2Mano.10.easy: The fortune teller pockets the coins and swears on the parrot that she will tell no one. The parrot, which heard it all, repeats at the market that same evening, in the fortune teller's voice, *"two lines, two lines"*, until someone throws a cloth over it.
G2Mano.10.short: The fortune teller swears to keep quiet. But the parrot repeats at the market: *"two lines, two lines"*.

G2Mano.12.full: You take her hand and tell her, in a solemn voice, that she has a son far away, a pain in her back and a secret concerning money. She laughs till she cries: you have guessed everything, because everyone, at her age, has a son far away, a pain in the back and a secret concerning money. "You have talent," she says. "But the two lines on your hand, I didn't make up."
G2Mano.12.easy: You take her hand and tell her gravely that she has a son far away, a bad back and a secret about money. She laughs till she cries: you have guessed it all, because everyone her age has a son far away, a bad back and a secret about money. "You have a gift," she says. "But I didn't make up the two lines on your hand."
G2Mano.12.short: You read her palm with the usual tricks, and she laughs. "You have a gift. But I didn't make up the two lines on your hand."

G2Contributo.2.full: With the last wire soldered, the second stage of the Telegraph comes to life. The glass jars light up with a milky glow, the bone keyboard vibrates, and the needle no longer trembles: it moves decisively from key to key and, for the first time, spells out a whole word.
G2Contributo.2.easy: When the last wire is soldered, the second part of the Telegraph switches on. The glass jars give a milk-white light, the bone keyboard vibrates and the needle no longer shakes: it moves surely from key to key and, for the first time, writes a whole word.
G2Contributo.2.short: With the last wire soldered, the Telegraph comes alive, and for the first time the needle spells a whole word.

G2Contributo.3.full: It is a name. No one in the family knows it; but the next morning, at the cemetery, they find it carved on a headstone the gravedigger swears he has never seen.
G2Contributo.3.easy: It is a name. No one in the family knows it. But the next morning, at the cemetery, they find it written on a headstone the gravedigger swears he has never seen.
G2Contributo.3.short: It is an unknown name. The next day they find it on a headstone no one had ever seen.

G2Contributo.4.full: Piece by piece, without waiting for anyone's consent, the first stage of the Telegraph is finally mounted against the laboratory wall. When you switch it on, the lamps throughout the house dim, and the needle, in its flask, begins to tremble. It is searching for a letter. It has not found it yet.
G2Contributo.4.easy: Piece by piece, without waiting for anyone's permission, the first part of the Telegraph is finally built against the laboratory wall. When you switch it on, the lights in the whole house get dimmer and the needle, inside the flask, starts to shake. It is looking for a letter. It cannot find it yet.
G2Contributo.4.short: On your own, you build the Telegraph's first stage. When you switch it on the needle trembles, seeking a letter it cannot yet find.

G2Contributo.5.full: You solder another length of wire, calibrate the needle, replace a cracked jar. The machine grows, but the needle stays still: pieces are still missing. As you put the tools away, you seem to hear a knock, impatient, from inside the flask.
G2Contributo.5.easy: You solder another piece of wire, adjust the needle, replace a broken jar. The machine grows, but the needle does not move: some pieces are still missing. As you put the tools away, you think you hear an impatient knock inside the flask.
G2Contributo.5.short: The machine grows, but the needle stays still. As you put the tools away, an impatient knock comes from the flask.

G2Contributo.6.full: You do not gain the Experiment's VP: instead, gain 1 Engineering Knowledge.

G2Fine.3.full: **THE MAYOR AND HIS FRIENDSHIPS.** Mayor Bódi, who inherited the office from his father as others inherit a watch, has long been ill and does not hide it. Nor does he hide that he is looking, among the notable families of {0}, for someone to protect in the years to come, and to be protected by in turn.
G2Fine.3.easy: **THE MAYOR AND HIS FRIENDS.** Mayor Bódi got his job from his father, the way other people inherit a watch. He has been ill for a long time and does not hide it. He also does not hide that he is looking, among the important families of {0}, for someone to protect in the coming years, who will protect him in return.
G2Fine.3.short: **THE MAYOR AND HIS FRIENDSHIPS.** Mayor Bódi, ill, is looking among the families of {0} for someone to protect, and be protected by.

G2Fine.4.full: Rumour has it that the families of the estate have already made their offers, in money and in favours. This newspaper is unable to confirm it, and its editor has been asked not to insist.
G2Fine.4.easy: People say the families of the estate have already made their offers, with money and favours. This newspaper cannot confirm it, and its editor has been asked not to ask questions.
G2Fine.4.short: They say the estate's families have already made their offers. The newspaper cannot confirm it.

G2Fine.5.full: It will be remembered that the late Father Anzelm, in his last year, repeatedly deplored this sort of dealing. Pending a new parish priest, the parish has been entrusted to the vicar of the neighbouring village, who has not yet expressed a view.
G2Fine.5.easy: It will be remembered that the late Father Anzelm, in his last year, often condemned this sort of business. Until a new parish priest is appointed, the parish is in the care of the vicar from the next village, who has not yet said anything.
G2Fine.5.short: Father Anzelm condemned such business. The vicar standing in for him has said nothing yet.

G2Fine.6.full: The village doctor, Dr Lukács, has made it known that he will support no candidate "who frequents little tables". His letter has been received with great interest and no consequences.
G2Fine.6.easy: The village doctor, Dr Lukács, has let it be known that he will support no candidate "who sits at little tables". His letter was received with great interest and no consequences.
G2Fine.6.short: Dr Lukács will support no one "who sits at little tables". No one takes any notice.

G2Fine.7.full: It is reported, finally, that the district's cemeteries, after the winter strike, have resumed normal service. Burials after sunset remain suspended "until further notice".
G2Fine.7.easy: Finally, the district's cemeteries have returned to normal service after the winter strike. Burials after sunset remain suspended "until further notice".
G2Fine.7.short: The cemeteries have reopened. But no one is buried after sunset any more.

G2Fine.8.full: Each player secretly takes in hand the money they wish to offer. When everyone is ready, reveal your offers together. Whoever offers the most pays and takes the **Mayor Coin**; the others take back their money.

G2SindacoMoneta.2.full: **{0}** takes the **Mayor Coin** from the **The Cost of Disease** Scenario Box. In the Third Generation, whoever has the Mayor Coin does not pay the extra $1 when visiting a Location that is already occupied.

G2Domande.2.full: The late years pass quickly, as they always do for those with too much to do. The fog rises and falls with the seasons, but never quite goes away: it withdraws into the ditches, the cemetery, behind the estate's greenhouses, and waits.
G2Domande.2.easy: The late years go by quickly, as always for people with too many things to do. The fog rises and falls with the seasons, but it never goes away completely: it hides in the ditches, in the cemetery, behind the estate's greenhouses, and waits.
G2Domande.2.short: The late years pass quickly. The fog never quite leaves: it withdraws into the ditches and the cemetery, and waits.

G2DomChiusura.3.full: The papers of the second generation also close with a series of funerals. I wanted to check the headstones in person, one by one, with a lantern, because in the fog of the cemetery (yes, it is still there) nothing could be read. The dates are those in the registers. But beneath each date, in smaller letters, the stonemason has also carved the hour; and all those hours fall between midnight and three.
G2DomChiusura.3.easy: The papers of the second generation also end with a series of funerals. I wanted to check the headstones myself, one by one, with a lantern, because in the fog of the cemetery (yes, it is still there) nothing could be read. The dates are the same as in the records. But under each date, in smaller letters, the hour is carved too. And all those hours are between midnight and three.
G2DomChiusura.3.short: The second generation also ends in the cemetery, in the fog. Under each date on the headstones an hour is carved: always between midnight and three.

G2DomChiusura.4.full: The stonemason, questioned by a colleague of mine in 1902, declared that he had never carved any hour.
G2DomChiusura.4.easy: The stonemason, questioned by a colleague of mine in 1902, said he had never carved any hour.

G2DomChiusura.5.full: Remove all pieces from the board and perform the End of the Generation. Return unused {icon:StorybookToken} tokens and the players' Charity tokens {icon:S1_HeartToken} to the supply. The Presences {icon:Creepy_Icon} return to the box.

G3Intro.3.full: LAST OF THE FAMILY BURIED YESTERDAY STOP ESTATE YOURS STOP NOTARY WAITING STOP DO NOT ARRIVE AFTER SUNSET STOP

G3Intro.4.full: The telegram reached the new heirs in distant cities, in offices, laboratories and colleges. When they stepped off the train (for now the train went there too) they found a small town that no longer resembled the village of the family stories: street lamps along the main road, a telegraph office, a bank with columns of imitation marble and, in the café on the square, a phonograph that played Viennese waltzes for anyone who dropped in a coin.
G3Intro.4.easy: The telegram reached the new heirs in faraway cities, in offices, laboratories, schools. When they got off the train (now the train went there too) they found a small town very different from the village of the family stories. There were street lamps along the main road, a telegraph office, a bank with fake marble columns and, in the café on the square, a phonograph that played Viennese waltzes for anyone who put in a coin.
G3Intro.4.short: The telegram reached the new heirs far away. Off the train, they found a modern little town: street lamps, a telegraph, a bank and a phonograph playing waltzes.

G3Citta.2.full: And there was the Circle. The Circle of the Last Hour no longer needed to hide, nor to advertise: it owned the undertaker's, half the buildings on the square and the majority of the town council. Its members wore a small silver eye in their buttonholes, and wore it with pride.
G3Citta.2.easy: And there was the Circle. The Circle of the Last Hour no longer had to hide, and did not need to make itself known: it owned the undertaker's, half the buildings on the square and most of the town council. Its members wore a small silver eye on their jackets, and were proud to wear it.
G3Citta.2.short: The Circle now owned the undertaker's, half the square and the town council. Its members proudly wore a silver eye.

G3Citta.3.full: And there was the Church. After years of sermons, trials and excommunications, the bishop had got what he wanted: the Circle of the Last Hour was outlawed, its séances a crime, and whoever spoke with the dead ended up before the church court. Father Benedek, Father Anzelm's successor, kept a register of names; the family's appeared in it more than once.
G3Citta.3.easy: And there was the Church. After years of sermons, trials and excommunications, the bishop had got what he wanted: the Circle of the Last Hour was banned, its séances were a crime, and anyone who spoke to the dead ended up before the Church court. Father Benedek, who had taken Father Anzelm's place, kept a list of names. The family's name was on it several times.
G3Citta.3.short: The Church had won: the Circle was outlawed and séances a crime. Father Benedek kept a register of names, and the family's appeared more than once.

G3Citta.4.full: And there was, still, the old war. The Circle of the Last Hour and the parish of Father Benedek, Father Anzelm's successor, fought over the souls of {0} one by one, with the tenacity of two neighbours quarrelling over a boundary wall. The wall, in this case, was the veil.
G3Citta.4.easy: And the old war was still going on. The Circle of the Last Hour and the parish of Father Benedek, who had taken Father Anzelm's place, fought over the souls of {0} one at a time, like two neighbours quarrelling over the wall between their land. In this case, the wall was the veil.
G3Citta.4.short: The Circle and Father Benedek's parish still fought over the souls of {0}, like neighbours over a boundary wall. The wall was the veil.

G3Citta.5.full: The Circle, however, was not dead: it still met, behind closed doors and with the best lawyers in the province, in its black marble Temple behind the town hall.
G3Citta.5.easy: The Circle, however, was not dead: it still met, behind closed doors and with the best lawyers in the province, in its black marble Temple behind the town hall.
G3Citta.5.short: But the Circle was not dead: it still met in secret, in its Temple behind the town hall.

G3Citta.6.full: The Circle's Temple, a low building of black marble behind the town hall, had been put up in the eighties, long after the woman of the caravan had left. Nobody knew whose money had paid for it. Everybody had an idea.
G3Citta.6.easy: The Circle's Temple, a low black marble building behind the town hall, had been built in the eighties, long after the woman of the caravan had left. No one knew whose money paid for it. Everyone had an idea.
G3Citta.6.short: The Circle's Temple had been built in the eighties. No one knew whose money paid for it, but everyone had an idea.

G3Citta.7.full: Madame Vámos, to hear people tell it, was the same age as fifty years before. No one knew where she lived. Everyone knew where to find her.
G3Citta.7.easy: People said that Madame Vámos was the same age as fifty years before. No one knew where she lived. Everyone knew where to find her.

G3Citta.8.full: Of Madame Vámos there remained a black shawl, displayed under glass in the Temple of the Circle, and an empty chair no one dared move.
G3Citta.8.easy: Of Madame Vámos there was only a black shawl, kept in a glass case in the Temple of the Circle, and an empty chair that no one dared to move.

G3Citta.9.full: On the first Sunday in town, the family:

G3Citta.12.full: Stays at home, unpacking the trunks.

G3Citta.13.full: The church is half full. Father Benedek celebrates hurriedly, his ears red with cold, and at the end comes to shake your hands on the steps, one by one, as one does with new parishioners. In the square, from the Circle's windows, someone is watching you.
G3Citta.13.easy: The church is half full. Father Benedek says Mass quickly, his ears red with cold, and afterwards comes to shake your hands on the steps, one by one, as with new parishioners. In the square, from the Circle's windows, someone is watching you.
G3Citta.13.short: Father Benedek shakes your hands like new parishioners. From the Circle's windows someone watches you.

G3Citta.15.full: The Circle's drawing room has velvet armchairs, electric lamps shaded in violet and a portrait from 1828 above the fireplace. They seat you in the front row, without asking who you are. During the séance the table knocks out your family's name, and two hundred people turn to look at you, smiling, the way one smiles at a relative who has arrived late for lunch.
G3Citta.15.easy: The Circle's hall has velvet armchairs, electric lamps with violet shades and a portrait from 1828 above the fireplace. They seat you in the front row, without asking who you are. During the séance the table knocks out your family's name, and two hundred people turn to look at you, smiling, as one smiles at a relative who is late for lunch.
G3Citta.15.short: At the séance the table knocks out your family's name. Two hundred people turn to smile at you.

G3Citta.17.full: You stay at the estate, among the trunks and the dust, opening windows nobody had opened for years. In the pockets of the coats hanging in the hall you find notes, pebbles, a dried carnation, a milk tooth. None of you throws anything away.
G3Citta.17.easy: You stay at the estate, among the trunks and the dust, opening windows no one had opened in years. In the pockets of the coats hanging in the hall you find notes, pebbles, a dried carnation, a milk tooth. None of you throws anything away.
G3Citta.17.short: You stay home. In the pockets of the old coats you find notes, pebbles, a dried carnation, a milk tooth.

G3Antenati.2.full: Now the family's dead are two generations. On the first night at the estate the knocking begins again, punctual as a clock, but denser: two different rhythms that overlap, interrupt and correct each other.
G3Antenati.2.easy: Now the family's dead are two generations. On the first night at the estate the knocking starts again, regular as a clock, but faster: two different rhythms that mix, interrupt and correct each other.
G3Antenati.2.short: On the first night the knocking returns, but now there are two rhythms, correcting each other.

G3Antenati.3.full: When the voices come, each heir hears two: that of their parent, and an older, fainter one, known only from portraits. They do not always agree.
G3Antenati.3.easy: When the voices come, each heir hears two: their parent's, and an older, weaker one that they know only from portraits. They do not always agree.
G3Antenati.3.short: Each heir hears two voices: a parent and an older ancestor. They do not always agree.

G3Antenati.4.full: Each player in turn reads their ancestors' message without showing it to the others. They may tell it, lie about it or keep quiet.

G3AntA.3.full: The two voices speak together, one over the other, about the same thing: a formula, an obsession, an idea that consumed two lives and now seeks a third. When one stops to draw breath, the other finishes the sentence.
G3AntA.3.easy: The two voices talk together, one over the other, about the same thing: a formula, an obsession, an idea that has used up two lives and now looks for a third. When one stops to breathe, the other finishes the sentence.
